## Literature Review: PIR/PHIST Tandem Expansions in *Plasmodium vivax*

This review focuses on literature from the past 10 years discussing the evolutionary genomics and pathogenesis of the PIR (including the *P. vivax*-specific VIR) and PHIST gene families. These multigene families are predominantly located in subtelomeric regions and are crucial for parasite immune evasion, host cell remodeling, and cytoadherence.

### Key Papers & Summaries

*   **[A new Plasmodium vivax reference sequence with improved assembly of the subtelomeres reveals an abundance of pir genes](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28008421/)** (2016)
    *   **Summary:** Long-read sequencing technologies were used to generate a highly contiguous *P. vivax* genome (P01). By accurately resolving the highly repetitive subtelomeric regions—which are notoriously difficult to sequence—the authors revealed a massive, previously underestimated tandem expansion of *pir* (*vir* in *P. vivax*) genes. This structural variation is central to the parasite's evolutionary genomics and capacity for antigenic variation.
    
*   **[Comparative clinical transcriptome of pir genes in severe Plasmodium vivax malaria](https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pntd.0013342)** (2024/2025)
    *   **Summary:** This study directly links the *vir* (*pir* superfamily) multigene family to severe *P. vivax* malaria pathogenesis. Through comparative clinical transcriptomics, the researchers demonstrated that the expression of these expanded genes mediates the parasite's capacity for immune system escape and cytoadherence, which exacerbates disease severity.

*   **[The Plasmodium PHIST and RESA-Like Protein Families of Human and Rodent Malaria Parasites](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0152510&type=printable)** (2016)
    *   **Summary:** This comparative genomic analysis tracks the expansion of the PHIST (*Plasmodium* helical interspersed subtelomeric) gene family across the genus. It highlights how human-infective parasites exhibit massive expansions (e.g., up to 65 paralogs) compared to rodent malaria models, suggesting a specialized evolutionary role in modifying the human erythrocyte during pathogenesis.

*   **[Plasmodium vivax-like genome sequences shed new insights into Plasmodium vivax biology and evolution](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30142149/)** (2018)
    *   **Summary:** By sequencing the closest genetic relative of *P. vivax* (found in African great apes), this study unravels the evolutionary history and host adaptation pathways of the parasite. It emphasizes how lineage-specific expansions of variant surface antigens, including the PIR/VIR families, drove the successful adaptation of *P. vivax* to human hosts.

*   **[De novo assembly of plasmodium interspersed repeat (pir) genes from Plasmodium vivax RNAseq data suggests geographic conservation of sub-family transcription](https://www.crick.ac.uk/research/publications/de-novo-assembly-of-plasmodium-interspersed-repeat-pir-genes-from-plasmodium-vivax-rnaseq-data-suggests-geographic-conservation-of-sub-family-transcription)** (2019)
    *   **Summary:** The authors bypassed the limits of incomplete reference genomes by assembling *pir* transcripts *de novo* from field isolates. They found that despite the rapid evolution and expansion of the *pir* gene family, specific sub-families exhibit geographically conserved transcriptional profiles, pointing to constrained, essential roles in *P. vivax* pathogenesis worldwide.

*   **[Differential Trafficking and Expression of PIR Proteins in Acute and Chronic Plasmodium Infections](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cellular-and-infection-microbiology/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2022.877253/full)** (2022)
    *   **Summary:** Focusing on the mechanistic role of the PIR protein family during pathogenesis, this paper explores how differential expression and cellular trafficking of these expanded proteins change between acute and chronic infection stages. While using a rodent model, the findings provide crucial functional context for the massive *pir* tandem expansions seen in *P. vivax*.

*   **[Structural and functional insights from detailed computational analysis of Plasmodium repetome](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12041-025-01516-x)** (2025)
    *   **Summary:** This recent paper conducts a wide computational survey of tandem repeats across *Plasmodium* proteomes, identifying *P. vivax* as exceptionally rich in these structural features. It discusses how the evolutionary expansion of tandem repeats in multigene families likely contributes to structural protein variations crucial for host-pathogen interactions and immune evasion.

## Literature Review: PIR/PHIST Tandem Expansions in *Plasmodium vivax*

This review focuses on literature from the past 10 years discussing the evolutionary genomics and pathogenesis of the PIR (including the *P. vivax*-specific VIR) and PHIST gene families. These multigene families are predominantly located in subtelomeric regions and are crucial for parasite immune evasion, host cell remodeling, and cytoadherence.

### Key Papers & Summaries

*   **[A new Plasmodium vivax reference sequence with improved assembly of the subtelomeres reveals an abundance of pir genes](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28008421/)** (2016)
    *   **Summary:** Long-read sequencing technologies were used to generate a highly contiguous *P. vivax* genome (P01). By accurately resolving the highly repetitive subtelomeric regions—which are notoriously difficult to sequence—the authors revealed a massive, previously underestimated tandem expansion of *pir* (*vir* in *P. vivax*) genes. This structural variation is central to the parasite's evolutionary genomics and capacity for antigenic variation.
    
*   **[Comparative clinical transcriptome of pir genes in severe Plasmodium vivax malaria](https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pntd.0013342)** (2024/2025)
    *   **Summary:** This study directly links the *vir* (*pir* superfamily) multigene family to severe *P. vivax* malaria pathogenesis. Through comparative clinical transcriptomics, the researchers demonstrated that the expression of these expanded genes mediates the parasite's capacity for immune system escape and cytoadherence, which exacerbates disease severity.

*   **[The Plasmodium PHIST and RESA-Like Protein Families of Human and Rodent Malaria Parasites](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0152510&type=printable)** (2016)
    *   **Summary:** This comparative genomic analysis tracks the expansion of the PHIST (*Plasmodium* helical interspersed subtelomeric) gene family across the genus. It highlights how human-infective parasites exhibit massive expansions (e.g., up to 65 paralogs) compared to rodent malaria models, suggesting a specialized evolutionary role in modifying the human erythrocyte during pathogenesis.

*   **[Plasmodium vivax-like genome sequences shed new insights into Plasmodium vivax biology and evolution](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30142149/)** (2018)
    *   **Summary:** By sequencing the closest genetic relative of *P. vivax* (found in African great apes), this study unravels the evolutionary history and host adaptation pathways of the parasite. It emphasizes how lineage-specific expansions of variant surface antigens, including the PIR/VIR families, drove the successful adaptation of *P. vivax* to human hosts.

*   **[De novo assembly of plasmodium interspersed repeat (pir) genes from Plasmodium vivax RNAseq data suggests geographic conservation of sub-family transcription](https://www.crick.ac.uk/research/publications/de-novo-assembly-of-plasmodium-interspersed-repeat-pir-genes-from-plasmodium-vivax-rnaseq-data-suggests-geographic-conservation-of-sub-family-transcription)** (2019)
    *   **Summary:** The authors bypassed the limits of incomplete reference genomes by assembling *pir* transcripts *de novo* from field isolates. They found that despite the rapid evolution and expansion of the *pir* gene family, specific sub-families exhibit geographically conserved transcriptional profiles, pointing to constrained, essential roles in *P. vivax* pathogenesis worldwide.

*   **[Differential Trafficking and Expression of PIR Proteins in Acute and Chronic Plasmodium Infections](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cellular-and-infection-microbiology/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2022.877253/full)** (2022)
    *   **Summary:** Focusing on the mechanistic role of the PIR protein family during pathogenesis, this paper explores how differential expression and cellular trafficking of these expanded proteins change between acute and chronic infection stages. While using a rodent model, the findings provide crucial functional context for the massive *pir* tandem expansions seen in *P. vivax*.

*   **[Structural and functional insights from detailed computational analysis of Plasmodium repetome](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12041-025-01516-x)** (2025)
    *   **Summary:** This recent paper conducts a wide computational survey of tandem repeats across *Plasmodium* proteomes, identifying *P. vivax* as exceptionally rich in these structural features. It discusses how the evolutionary expansion of tandem repeats in multigene families likely contributes to structural protein variations crucial for host-pathogen interactions and immune evasion.

---

## Gene and Protein Structures

### PIR (Plasmodium Interspersed Repeat) / VIR
* **Gene Structure:** The *pir* genes typically share a highly conserved three-exon structure across different *Plasmodium* species:
  * **Exon 1:** A short sequence that encodes a signal peptide, directing the protein into the secretory pathway.
  * **Exon 2:** A long, highly variable exon encoding the bulk of the extracellular domain (ectodomain) responsible for antigenic variation.
  * **Exon 3:** Encodes the transmembrane domain and a short cytoplasmic tail, anchoring the protein to membranes.
* **Protein Structure:** Recent structural biology (e.g., Harrison & Higgins, 2020) resolved the *pir* ectodomain, showing that despite immense sequence variation, the proteins maintain a conserved structural fold. The core consists of beta-strands and alpha-helices organized into a unique scaffold that can tolerate massive amino acid substitutions. This allows the parasite to continuously change its surface "appearance" to immune cells while keeping the protein structurally sound.
* **Function:** VIR/PIR proteins are exported to the surface of the infected red blood cell. By constantly switching which *vir* variants are expressed, the parasite evades the host’s humoral (antibody) immune response. They also play major roles in cytoadherence (making infected red blood cells sticky so they attach to the host's endothelium and avoid clearance in the spleen) and rosetting (binding uninfected red blood cells). In *P. vivax*, *vir* genes are heavily implicated in severe malaria pathogenesis by enabling the parasite to establish chronic, stealthy infections.

### PHIST (Plasmodium Helical Interspersed Subtelomeric)
* **Gene Structure:** Like *pir*, *phist* genes are primarily located in the hyper-recombinogenic subtelomeric regions of the parasite's chromosomes, which facilitates rapid gene duplication and tandem expansion. Most *phist* members include a signal sequence and a *Plasmodium* Export Element (PEXEL) motif, which acts as a targeting signal to export the protein out of the parasite and into the host erythrocyte.
* **Protein Structure:** The defining feature of PHIST proteins is the **PHIST domain**, a conserved region of approximately 150 amino acids. Structurally, this domain consists of four consecutive alpha-helices with conserved aromatic residues. The domain itself does not possess known enzymatic activity; rather, it acts as a critical protein-protein interaction module.
* **Function:** PHIST proteins are essentially the "scaffold builders" and "anchors" inside the infected human red blood cell. Once exported, they localize to the host cell cytoskeleton or to membranous structures called Maurer's clefts. Their primary function is to remodel the host cell. Crucially, they bind to major virulence factors (like PfEMP1 in *P. falciparum* or its equivalents) and anchor them securely to the red blood cell's cytoskeleton (specifically interacting with human host proteins like band 4.1R). Without PHIST proteins securely anchoring these surface antigens, the infected red blood cell cannot properly adhere to blood vessel walls, drastically reducing the parasite's virulence.

**PIR/VIR:**
*   **Gene:** Typically a conserved 3-exon structure (Exon 1: signal peptide, Exon 2: highly variable antigenic ectodomain, Exon 3: transmembrane anchor).
*   **Protein:** The ectodomain has a unique, highly conserved folding scaffold that can tolerate massive amino acid variation, allowing endless "disguises." 
*   **Function:** Exported to the surface of the infected red blood cell. They mediate immune evasion (antigenic variation), cytoadherence (sticking to blood vessels), and rosetting (clumping blood cells together) to avoid spleen clearance.

**PHIST:**
*   **Gene:** Located in subtelomeres (promoting tandem duplication) and usually contains a PEXEL motif that flags the protein for export into the host cell.
*   **Protein:** Defined by the ~150 amino acid "PHIST domain," which consists of four consecutive alpha-helices acting as a protein-protein interaction module.
*   **Function:** These are internal "scaffolders." They remodel the host red blood cell's cytoskeleton from the inside. They act as the vital anchors that grab major virulence factors and tether them tightly to the host cell membrane so the cell can successfully stick to blood vessel walls.

edits.newText:
### PHIST (Plasmodium Helical Interspersed Subtelomeric)
* **Gene Structure:** Like many *Plasmodium* exported protein families, *phist* genes are primarily located in the hyper-recombinogenic subtelomeric regions and typically share a conserved **two-exon structure**:
  * **Exon 1:** A short sequence that encodes a hydrophobic signal peptide for initial entry into the parasite's secretory pathway.
  * **Exon 2:** A much larger exon that usually begins with a *Plasmodium* Export Element (PEXEL) motif—a targeting signal to export the protein into the host erythrocyte—followed by the sequence encoding the defining PHIST domain and the rest of the protein.
* **Protein Structure:** The defining feature of PHIST proteins is the **PHIST domain**, a conserved region of approximately 150 amino acids. Structurally, this domain consists of four consecutive alpha-helices with conserved aromatic residues. The domain itself does not possess known enzymatic activity; rather, it acts as a critical protein-protein interaction module.

 34   * **Exon 1:** A short sequence that encodes a signal peptide, directing the protein into the secretory pathway.
 35   * **Exon 2:** A long, highly variable exon encoding the bulk of the extracellular domain (ectodomain) responsible for antigenic variation.
 36   * **Exon 3:** Encodes the transmembrane domain and a short cytoplasmic tail, anchoring the protein to membranes.

The core consists of beta-strands and alpha-helices organized into a unique scaffold that can tolerate massive amino acid substitutions. This allows the parasite to continuously change its surface "appearance" to immune cells while keeping the protein structurally sound.
 38 * **Function:** VIR/PIR proteins are exported to the surface of the infected red blood cell. By constantly switching which *vir* variants are expressed, the parasite evades the host’s humoral (antibody) immune response. They also play major roles in cytoadherence (making infected red blood cells sticky so they attach to the host's endothelium and avoid clearance in the spleen) and rosetting (binding uninfected red blood cells). In *P. vivax*, *vir* genes are heavily implicated in severe malaria pathogenesis by enabling the parasite to establish chronic, stealthy infections.

There are two prominent modern *Plasmodium vivax* assemblies available on NCBI that were built using long-read sequencing technologies (PacBio):

1. **PvPAM (GCA_949152365.1)**: Published in 2023, this is a highly complete South American reference genome sourced from the Peruvian Amazon. It was sequenced using **PacBio** and was able to fully resolve the telomeric ends of 17 out of 28 chromosomal ends.
2. **PvW1 (GCA_914969965.1)**: Published in 2021, this is a **hybrid assembly (PacBio + Illumina)** of a *P. vivax* clone used in controlled human malaria infection studies. It rivals the standard PvP01 assembly in completeness and has very few unassigned scaffolds.

*(Note: The widely used **PvP01** reference genome, which was the first to accurately reveal the massive >1,000 copy expansion of the *pir* gene family compared to the old Sanger-based Salvador-I genome, was actually assembled using very high-depth **Illumina** sequencing, rather than PacBio or Nanopore.)*

urls.content:
## Abstract

### Background

_Plasmodium vivax_ is the second most important cause of human malaria worldwide, and accounts for the majority of malaria cases in South America. A high-quality reference genome exists for Papua Indonesia (PvP01) and Thailand (PvW1), but is lacking for South America. A reference genome specifically for South America would be beneficial though, as _P. vivax_ is a genetically diverse parasite with geographical clustering.

### Results

This study presents a new high-quality assembly of a South American _P. vivax_ isolate, referred to as PvPAM (_P. vivax_ Peruvian AMazon). The genome was obtained from a low input patient sample from the Peruvian Amazon and sequenced using PacBio technology, resulting in a highly complete assembly with 6497 functional genes. Telomeric ends were present in 17 out of 28 chromosomal ends, and additional (sub)telomeric regions are present in 12 unassigned contigs. A comparison of multigene families between PvPAM and the PvP01 genome revealed remarkable variation in _vir_ genes, and the presence of merozoite surface proteins (MSP) 3.6 and 3.7. Three _dhfr_ and _dhps_ drug resistance associated mutations are present in PvPAM, similar to those found in other Peruvian isolates. Mapping of publicly available South American whole genome sequencing (WGS) data to PvPAM resulted in significantly fewer variants and truncated reads compared to the use of PvP01 or PvW1 as reference genomes. To minimize the number of core genome variants in non-South American samples, PvW1 is most suited for Southeast Asian isolates, both PvPAM and PvW1 are suited for South Asian isolates, and PvPAM is recommended for African isolates. Interestingly, non-South American samples still contained the least subtelomeric variants when mapped to PvPAM, indicating high quality of the PvPAM subtelomeric regions.

### Conclusions

Our findings show that the PvPAM reference genome more accurately represents South American _P. vivax_ isolates in comparison to PvP01 and PvW1. In addition, PvPAM has a high level of completeness, and contains a similar number of annotated genes as PvP01 or PvW1. The PvPAM genome therefore will be a valuable resource to improve future genomic analyses on _P. vivax_ isolates from the South American continent.

## Background

_Plasmodium vivax_ is the second most common cause of malaria in humans after _P. falciparum_. _P. vivax_ is widespread outside of Africa, accounting there for one-third of the malaria infections [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR1 "WHO. World malaria report. In. Geneva: WHO; 2021.")]. Due to the absence of a continuous culturing system [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR2 "Bermúdez M, Moreno-Pérez DA, Arévalo-Pinzón G, Curtidor H, Patarroyo MA. Plasmodium vivax in vitro continuous culture: the spoke in the wheel. Malar J. 2018;17(301):1–12.")] and the former assumption that _P. vivax_ infections are benign [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR3 "Howes RE, Battle KE, Mendis KN, Smith DL, Cibulskis RE, Baird JK, Hay SI. Global epidemiology of Plasmodium vivax. Am J Trop Med Hyg. 2016;95(6 Suppl):15–34.")], _P. vivax_ research has been lagging behind that of _P. falciparum_. Only in 2008, the first _P. vivax_ reference genome, Salvador I, was assembled [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR4 "Carlton JM, Adams JH, Silva JC, Bidwell SL, Lorenzi H, Caler E, Crabtree J, Angiuoli SV, Merino EF, Amedeo P, et al. Comparative genomics of the neglected human malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. Nature. 2008;455(7214):757–63.")], while the _P. falciparum_ 3D7 reference genome was already published in 2002 [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR5 "Gardner MJ, Hall N, Fung E, White O, Berriman M, Hyman RW, Carlton JM, Pain A, Nelson KE, Bowman S, et al. Genome sequence of the human malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Nature. 2002;419(6906):498–511.")].

Hitherto, several _P. vivax_ genomes have been assembled for _P. vivax_. The Salvador I (PvSalI) genome was assembled from paired-read Sanger sequencing data, coming from an El Salvador isolate that was passaged in _Saimiri_ monkeys [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR4 "Carlton JM, Adams JH, Silva JC, Bidwell SL, Lorenzi H, Caler E, Crabtree J, Angiuoli SV, Merino EF, Amedeo P, et al. Comparative genomics of the neglected human malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. Nature. 2008;455(7214):757–63."), [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR6 "Collins WE, Contacos PG, Krotoski WA, Howard WA. Transmission of four central american strains of Plasmodium vivax from monkey to man. J Parasitol. 1972;58(2):332–5.")]. However, it contains > 2000 unassigned contigs that were not assigned to a chromosome, making it less suited for alignment of whole genome sequencing (WGS) data. Similarly, Illumina-based assemblies from four monkey-passaged isolates from Brazil, India, Mauritania and North Korea [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR7 "Neafsey DE, Galinsky K, Jiang RHY, Young L, Sykes SM, Saif S, Gujja S, Goldberg JM, Young S, Zeng Q, et al. The malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax exhibits greater genetic diversity than Plasmodium falciparum. Nat Genet. 2012;44(9):1046–50.")] and 1 Cambodian field isolate [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR8 "Hester J, Chan ER, Menard D, Mercereau-Puijalon O, Barnwell J, Zimmerman PA, Serre D. De novo assembly of a field isolate genome reveals novel Plasmodium vivax erythrocyte invasion genes. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2013;7(12):e2569.")] were highly fragmented, with > 1500 scaffolds. More recently, Auburn et al. (2016) released a high-quality reference genome from an Illumina-sequenced Papua Indonesian isolate (PvP01), along with two draft assemblies from Thailand (PvT01) and China (PvC01). Finally, a Thai isolate used in controlled human infections was long-read sequenced with PacBio, resulting in the high-quality PvW1 reference genome [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465.")].

South America is not yet represented by the existing high-quality reference genomes (PvP01, PvW1), although the majority of the malaria cases in this continent are _P. vivax_ [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR1 "WHO. World malaria report. In. Geneva: WHO; 2021.")]. Since _P. vivax_ is genetically more diverse than _P. falciparum_ [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR7 "Neafsey DE, Galinsky K, Jiang RHY, Young L, Sykes SM, Saif S, Gujja S, Goldberg JM, Young S, Zeng Q, et al. The malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax exhibits greater genetic diversity than Plasmodium falciparum. Nat Genet. 2012;44(9):1046–50."), [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR10 "Fola AA, Harrison GA, Hazairin MH, Barnadas C, Hetzel MW, Iga J, Siba PM, Mueller I, Barry AE. Higher complexity of infection and genetic diversity of Plasmodium vivax than Plasmodium falciparum across all malaria transmission zones of Papua New Guinea. Am J Trop Med Hyg. 2017;96(3):630–41."), [11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR11 "Hupalo DN, Luo Z, Melnikov A, Sutton PL, Rogov P, Escalante A, Vallejo AF, Herrera S, Arévalo-Herrera M, Fan Q, et al. Population genomics studies identify signatures of global dispersal and drug resistance in Plasmodium vivax. Nat Genet. 2016;48(8):953–8.")], there is a strong geographical differentiation between isolates from different continents [[11](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR11 "Hupalo DN, Luo Z, Melnikov A, Sutton PL, Rogov P, Escalante A, Vallejo AF, Herrera S, Arévalo-Herrera M, Fan Q, et al. Population genomics studies identify signatures of global dispersal and drug resistance in Plasmodium vivax. Nat Genet. 2016;48(8):953–8."),[12](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR12 "Benavente ED, Manko E, Phelan J, Campos M, Nolder D, Fernandez D, Velez-Tobon G, Castaño AT, Dombrowski JG, Marinho CRF, et al. Distinctive genetic structure and selection patterns in Plasmodium vivax from South Asia and East Africa. Nat Commun. 2021;12(1):3160."),[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR13 "Koepfli C, Rodrigues PT, Antao T, Orjuela-Sánchez P, Van den Eede P, Gamboa D, Van Hong N, Bendezu J, Erhart A, Barnadas C, et al. Plasmodium vivax diversity and population structure across four continents. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2015;9(6):e0003872.")]. The PvP01 and PvW1 assemblies originate from Papua Indonesia and Thailand, and isolates from these countries are genetically distant from the South American ones [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR12 "Benavente ED, Manko E, Phelan J, Campos M, Nolder D, Fernandez D, Velez-Tobon G, Castaño AT, Dombrowski JG, Marinho CRF, et al. Distinctive genetic structure and selection patterns in Plasmodium vivax from South Asia and East Africa. Nat Commun. 2021;12(1):3160.")]. Therefore, a new _P. vivax_ reference genome from South American origin could improve variant calling of South American isolates and provide more accurate information on indels (insertions and deletions) and large structural variants. Especially these large structural variants cannot be detected readily by aligning short-read sequences to a reference genome, which is why continent-specific reference genomes are expected to increase mapping quality and reveal new or missing genes. This will have a greater impact in the subtelomeric regions, which are highly dynamic with frequent duplication and recombination events [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR14 "Mok BW, Ribacke U, Sherwood E, Wahlgren M. A highly conserved segmental duplication in the subtelomeres of Plasmodium falciparum chromosomes varies in copy number. Malar J. 2008;7(1):1–9.")], and contain important multigene families involved in immune evasion and host-parasite interactions [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR4 "Carlton JM, Adams JH, Silva JC, Bidwell SL, Lorenzi H, Caler E, Crabtree J, Angiuoli SV, Merino EF, Amedeo P, et al. Comparative genomics of the neglected human malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. Nature. 2008;455(7214):757–63.")]. In addition, accurate reflection of the sample’s structural variants in the reference genome can help the assessment of RNA isoforms, which are known to be abundant in _P. vivax_ [[15](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR15 "Zhu L, Mok S, Imwong M, Jaidee A, Russell B, Nosten F, Day NP, White NJ, Preiser PR, Bozdech Z. New insights into the Plasmodium vivax transcriptome using RNA-Seq. Sci Rep. 2016;6(1):20498."),[16](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR16 "Kim A, Popovici J, Vantaux A, Samreth R, Bin S, Kim S, Roesch C, Liang L, Davies H, Felgner P, et al. Characterization of P. vivax blood stage transcriptomes from field isolates reveals similarities among infections and complex gene isoforms. Sci Rep. 2017;7(1):7761."),[17](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR17 "Siegel SV, Chappell L, Hostetler JB, Amaratunga C, Suon S, Bohme U, Berriman M, Fairhurst RM, Rayner JC. Analysis of Plasmodium vivax schizont transcriptomes from field isolates reveals heterogeneity of expression of genes involved in host-parasite interactions. Sci Rep. 2020;10(1):16667."),[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR18 "Hazzard B, Sá JM, Ellis AC, Pascini TV, Amin S, Wellems TE, Serre D. Long read single cell RNA sequencing reveals the isoform diversity of Plasmodium vivax transcripts. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2022;16(12):e0010991.")].

Since _de novo_ assembly of a reference genome makes use of the overlaps between sequenced fragments (reads), longer reads improve confidence and quality of the assembly. In addition, long reads can better resolve repetitive or low-complexity regions often found in the subtelomeres. Short-read technologies like Illumina typically have read lengths of 50–300 bases, while Pacific Biosciences SMRT technology (PacBio) and Oxford Nanopore technology (ONT), the leading long-read sequencing technologies to date, readily exceed 10,000 bases. Therefore, PacBio and Nanopore are more suited for reference genome sequencing. At the moment of writing, PacBio sequencing has an accuracy of 99.8% [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR19 "Wenger AM, Peluso P, Rowell WJ, Chang P-C, Hall RJ, Concepcion GT, Ebler J, Fungtammasan A, Kolesnikov A, Olson ND, et al. Accurate circular consensus long-read sequencing improves variant detection and assembly of a human genome. Nat Biotechnol. 2019;37(10):1155–62.")], similar to what can be achieved with Illumina sequencing, and higher than the 99% that can be reached with the Nanopore R10.4 chemistry [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR20 "Sereika M, Kirkegaard RH, Karst SM, Michaelsen TY, Sørensen EA, Wollenberg RD, Albertsen M. Oxford Nanopore R10.4 long-read sequencing enables the generation of near-finished bacterial genomes from pure cultures and metagenomes without short-read or reference polishing. Nat Methods. 2022;19(7):823–6.")]. Due to PacBio’s use of circular consensus sequencing (a circular read is sequenced multiple times), random sequencing errors are largely removed [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR19 "Wenger AM, Peluso P, Rowell WJ, Chang P-C, Hall RJ, Concepcion GT, Ebler J, Fungtammasan A, Kolesnikov A, Olson ND, et al. Accurate circular consensus long-read sequencing improves variant detection and assembly of a human genome. Nat Biotechnol. 2019;37(10):1155–62.")]. Although a bias for indels at homopolymer regions remains [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR19 "Wenger AM, Peluso P, Rowell WJ, Chang P-C, Hall RJ, Concepcion GT, Ebler J, Fungtammasan A, Kolesnikov A, Olson ND, et al. Accurate circular consensus long-read sequencing improves variant detection and assembly of a human genome. Nat Biotechnol. 2019;37(10):1155–62."), [21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR21 "Karst SM, Ziels RM, Kirkegaard RH, Sørensen EA, McDonald D, Zhu Q, Knight R, Albertsen M. High-accuracy long-read amplicon sequences using unique molecular identifiers with Nanopore or PacBio sequencing. Nat Methods. 2021;18(2):165–9.")], it is the most robust long-read sequencing method to date, which was also used to construct the Thai PvW1 reference [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465.")]. The PvW1 sample was obtained from controlled human malaria infections, which allows extraction of a high amount of input DNA. However, low input protocols are becoming more common, and PacBio recently released their Ultra-Low DNA Input protocol (5–20 ng DNA) [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR22 "Ultra-Low DNA. Input Workflow for SMRT Sequencing [
                  https://www.pacb.com/plant-animal-biology/introducing-the-ultra-low-input-protocol-for-smrt-sequencing/
                  
                ].")]. This provides opportunities to long-read sequence _P. vivax_ DNA from low blood volume and/or low parasitaemia patient samples, which is common in natural human infections.

In this study, a leukocyte-depleted blood sample from a _P. vivax_ patient from the Peruvian Amazon was sequenced with PacBio using the Ultra-Low DNA Input protocol, allowing the assembly of a new and high-quality South American reference genome named PvPAM (_P. vivax_ Peruvian AMazon). The PvPAM chromosomes have a high level of completeness (telomeric repeats in 17/28 chromosomal ends), although 12 unassigned contigs remain. A variant analysis of publicly available WGS data shows that the PvPAM core genome represents South American and African isolates better than the PvP01 and PvW1 reference genomes. In the subtelomeric regions, the use of PvPAM as a reference genome resulted in a significantly lower number of variants for WGS data from all continents, outperforming PvP01 and PvW1.

## Results

### Construction of a high-quality reference genome from a low-input _P. vivax_ patient DNA sample

A new reference genome was constructed from a monoclonal _P. vivax_ patient sample originating from the Peruvian Amazon basin (Iquitos), which we named PvPAM (_P. vivax_ Peruvian AMazon). Although the input sample contained a very low amount of parasite DNA (9 ng), the PacBio Ultra-Low Input protocol for library preparation allowed to sequence the _P. vivax_ genome in high depth and enabled to build a high-quality reference genome for the South American Amazon region.

497 billion raw continuous long read (CLR) bases were sequenced, and after pre-processing, 24.5 billion high fidelity circular consensus sequencing (CCS) read bases were left, with reads being 10,670 bases long on average. When mapped to the PvP01 reference genome, this resulted in an average sequencing depth of 821x. This is well above the recommended 15x depth for assembly of a haploid genome [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR23 "PacBio. Application note - considerations for using the low and ultra-low DNA input workflows for whole genome sequencing V2. In.; 2020: 12.")], but due to the repetitive and AT-rich subtelomeric regions, higher depths are necessary to fully assemble the eukaryotic _P. vivax_ genome.

Genome assembly and subsequent scaffolding resulted in 14 chromosomes, of which 4 were completely assembled, while the other 10 were scaffolds consisting of 2–4 contigs. The gaps between those contigs were patched based on the PvP01 and PvW1 reference genomes [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465."), [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR24 "Auburn S, Böhme U, Steinbiss S, Trimarsanto H, Hostetler J, Sanders M, Gao Q, Nosten F, Newbold CI, Berriman M et al. A new Plasmodium vivax reference sequence with improved assembly of the subtelomeres reveals an abundance of pir genes. Wellcome open Research 2016, 1(4).")]. The patches had a median length of 388 bases (range 41-2592 bases) (Supplementary Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)), which indicates that the initial PvPAM assembly was of good quality and only few bases were uncovered. Further polishing of the genome with Illumina reads, obtained in parallel from the PvPAM isolate, introduced some PvPAM-specific changes in the patched regions. In addition to the 14 chromosomes, 12 contigs could not be uniquely assigned to any chromosome, although they were identified as subtelomeric based on their low GC content (< 25%) and presence of _vir_ (variant interspersed repeat) genes.

PvPAM chromosome-completeness was assessed by the presence of telomeric CCCT(A/G)AA repeats [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR25 "Ponzi M, Pace T, Dore E, Frontali C. Identification of a telomeric DNA sequence in Plasmodium berghei. EMBO J. 1985;4(11):2991–5."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR26 "Vernick KD, McCutchan TF. Sequence and structure of a Plasmodium falciparum telomere. Mol Biochem Parasitol. 1988;28(2):85–94.")], which indicate that the chromosome was fully assembled up to the 5’ or 3’ end. Telomeric repeats were only observed at one chromosomal end in PvP01, while they are present in 17/28 chromosomal ends in the PvPAM, indicating a higher number of completely assembled chromosomes (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)). Eight additional telomeric repeat sequences could be found in the 12 unassigned and subtelomeric PvPAM contigs.

### Structural comparison of PvPAM to the PvP01 and PvW1 reference genomes

PvPAM was compared on a structural and annotation level to the two highest quality _P. vivax_ reference genomes existing to date: PvP01 [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR24 "Auburn S, Böhme U, Steinbiss S, Trimarsanto H, Hostetler J, Sanders M, Gao Q, Nosten F, Newbold CI, Berriman M et al. A new Plasmodium vivax reference sequence with improved assembly of the subtelomeres reveals an abundance of pir genes. Wellcome open Research 2016, 1(4).")] and the PacBio-based PvW1 [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465.")]. These three reference genomes have overall similar genome sizes (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab1)). However, whole genome alignments of the reference genomes reveal that most PvPAM chromosomes contain longer subtelomeric regions than their PvP01 counterparts (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)A). This is because large parts of the PvP01 subtelomeric regions are divided over many short contigs that are not assigned to any chromosome, while the PvPAM reference genome is less fragmented. The subtelomeric regions of the PvW1 chromosomes are overall of similar length as in PvPAM (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab1)), but at the chromosome level, the subtelomeres often have different lengths or do not fully align (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)B). We determined core genome boundaries based on GC-content and sequence identity between PvPAM, PvP01 and PvW1. These borders show that the PvW1 and PvPAM chromosomes possess longer subtelomeric regions than the PvP01 chromosomes, due to higher contiguity in PacBio-based genomes (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab1)).

The PvPAM genome contains 6497 functional genes (i.e., genes not annotated as a pseudogene), a higher number than found in PvW1, but still less than in PvP01 (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab1)). Out of the 6497 functional genes, 1109 are not present in PvP01. Of those, 487 genes cannot be linked to any PvP01 gene through orthology, and are therefore new in the PvPAM reference genome (Supplementary Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)). The number of PvPAM pseudogenes is higher than what was observed for PvP01 (4.7% vs. 2.7% of all genes). Pseudogenes are mainly located in the subtelomeres (89% of PvPAM and 95% of PvP01 pseudogenes), due to the dynamic nature of this region [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR14 "Mok BW, Ribacke U, Sherwood E, Wahlgren M. A highly conserved segmental duplication in the subtelomeres of Plasmodium falciparum chromosomes varies in copy number. Malar J. 2008;7(1):1–9.")]. In the PvPAM mitochondrial and apicoplast genome, less functional genes were annotated in comparison to PvP01. In the apicoplast, this is partly due to its shorter length in PvPAM (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)D). However, the PvPAM apicoplast and mitochondrial genome are highly similar to PvP01 (Figs.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)C-D and 89.1% and 99.9% pairwise identity with MUSCLE, respectively), and missing gene annotations are attributed to a limitation of the Companion annotation tool.

### PvPAM multigene families in subtelomeric or internally variable regions

Multigene families located at the subtelomeres or internally variable regions often play an important role in host-parasite interactions, immune response and pathogenicity, and can vary in (pseudo)gene number across isolates due to the dynamic nature of subtelomeres [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR4 "Carlton JM, Adams JH, Silva JC, Bidwell SL, Lorenzi H, Caler E, Crabtree J, Angiuoli SV, Merino EF, Amedeo P, et al. Comparative genomics of the neglected human malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. Nature. 2008;455(7214):757–63.")]. In particular, the _P. vivax_ variant genes (_vir_) are known to be involved in immune invasion, and the _P. vivax_ tryptophan-rich antigens (PvTRAg), _P. vivax_ reticulocyte binding proteins (PvRBP) and _P. vivax_ merozoite surface proteins (MSP) take part in invasion or red blood cell (RBC) binding.

In the PvPAM genome, 975 + 99 _vir_ genes (functional genes + pseudogenes) were found, which is less than the 1093 + 116 in PvP01 and 1145 functional _vir_ genes in PvW1. Remarkably, out of these 975 functional _vir_ genes identified in PvPAM, only 370 have been transferred from the PvP01 reference genome through sequence similarity. The remaining 605 _vir_ genes are newly predicted in PvPAM.

All 40 _PvTRAg_ genes present in PvP01 were also found in PvPAM. No additional PvPAM _PvTRAg_’s were discovered based on othology groups (OrthoMCL) or the presence of the _Plasmodium_ tryptophan-rich protein Pfam domain (PF12319). _PvTRAg36_ (PVP01_0000140), which was reported to bind to the band 3 and basigin RBC receptors [[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR27 "Zeeshan M, Tyagi RK, Tyagi K, Alam MS, Sharma YD. Host-parasite interaction: selective Pv-fam-a family proteins of Plasmodium vivax bind to a restricted number of human erythrocyte receptors. J Infect Dis. 2014;211(7):1111–20."), [28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR28 "Alam MS, Zeeshan M, Rathore S, Sharma YD. Multiple Plasmodium vivax proteins of Pv-fam-a family interact with human erythrocyte receptor Band 3 and have a role in red cell invasion. Biochem Biophys Res Commun. 2016;478(3):1211–6.")], is annotated as a pseudogene in PvPAM. However, pseudogene annotation is based on prediction models. The utilization of an alternative translation start site and the splicing out of an intron (as seen in PvP01 _PvTRAg36_) would result in a fully functional PvTRAg36 protein. The more complete PvPAM assembly also enabled to locate 10 _PvTRAg_’s to chromosome 13, that were formerly annotated to the unassigned contigs ‘Transfer.PvP01_00_1.final’ (PvP01) and ‘CAJZCX010000017’ (PvW1).

Furthermore, the PvPAM genome contains all 5 full length _PvRBP_ genes that are present in PvP01. Out of the 3 partial _PvRBP_ genes that were identified in PvP01 and PvSalI, _PvRBP1-p1_ (PVP01_0010770) and _PvRBP2-p2_ (PVX_101590) are absent in PvPAM (Supplementary Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)). _PvRBP2-p2_ was reported to be present only in a subset of _P. vivax_ samples, and is also absent in PvP01 [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR29 "Hietanen J, Chim-Ong A, Chiramanewong T, Gruszczyk J, Roobsoong W, Tham W-H, Sattabongkot J, Nguitragool W. Gene models, expression repertoire, and immune response of Plasmodium vivax reticulocyte binding proteins. Infect Immun. 2016;84(3):677–85.")]. Of the 3 _PvRBP_ pseudogenes in PvP01, _PvRBP3_ and the isolate-specific _PvRBP2e_ [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR8 "Hester J, Chan ER, Menard D, Mercereau-Puijalon O, Barnwell J, Zimmerman PA, Serre D. De novo assembly of a field isolate genome reveals novel Plasmodium vivax erythrocyte invasion genes. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2013;7(12):e2569.")] are identified in PvPAM. The PvP01 _PvRBP2d_ pseudogene is replaced by 3 partial genes in PvPAM, while in PvW1 it consists of 2 partial genes (alignment in Supplementary Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1), Supplementary Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)). Further studies are required to confirm whether some isolates indeed show several shorter (partial) PvRBP2d proteins, or whether this is an annotation model artefact and in reality is one long pseudogene. No additional _PvRBP_ genes were discovered in PvPAM based on orthology clusters or Pfam domains (PF16830, PF18515).

Additionally, multigene families that are located in tandem on hypervariable regions in the core genome, such as PvMSP3, PvMSP7 and the _P. vivax_ serine-repeat antigens (PvSERA), have the potential to vary in number of genes [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR30 "Pearson RD, Amato R, Auburn S, Miotto O, Almagro-Garcia J, Amaratunga C, Suon S, Mao S, Noviyanti R, Trimarsanto H, et al. Genomic analysis of local variation and recent evolution in Plasmodium vivax. Nat Genet. 2016;48(8):959–64.")]. The _PvMSP3_ genes are highly polymorphic [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR31 "Ford A, Kepple D, Abagero BR, Connors J, Pearson R, Auburn S, Getachew S, Ford C, Gunalan K, Miller LH, et al. Whole genome sequencing of Plasmodium vivax isolates reveals frequent sequence and structural polymorphisms in erythrocyte binding genes. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2020;14(10):e0008234.")], and have been shown to have a varying number of genes at the center of the gene cluster [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465.")]. Indeed, PvPAM contains two more centrally located _MSP3_ genes (_MSP3.6_, _MSP3.7_) that are absent in PvP01 and PvW1, a feature it shares with the Central-American PvSalI. On the other hand, PvSalI’s _MSP3.4_ is missing in PvPAM (Supplementary Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)). There was no variation in the number of genes observed in the _PvMSP7_ and _PvSERA_ families between PvPAM and PvP01.

Although not located in the subtelomeres or internally variable regions, the erythrocyte binding–like (EBL) superfamily is also involved in invasion. Its best known member, the _P. vivax_ Duffy binding protein (PvDBP), binds to the Duffy receptor to enable reticulocyte invasion [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR32 "Barnwell JW, Nichols ME, Rubinstein P. In vitro evaluation of the role of the Duffy blood group in erythrocyte invasion by Plasmodium vivax. J Exp Med. 1989;169(5):1795–802.")]. _PvDBP_ copy number variations have been associated with immune evasion [[33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR33 "Hostetler JB, Lo E, Kanjee U, Amaratunga C, Suon S, Sreng S, Mao S, Yewhalaw D, Mascarenhas A, Kwiatkowski DP, et al. Independent origin and global distribution of distinct Plasmodium vivax Duffy binding protein gene duplications. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2016;10(10):e0005091."), [34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR34 "Popovici J, Roesch C, Carias LL, Khim N, Kim S, Vantaux A, Mueller I, Chitnis CE, King CL, Witkowski B. Amplification of Duffy binding protein-encoding gene allows Plasmodium vivax to evade host anti-DBP humoral immunity. Nat Commun. 2020;11(1):953.")], but no additional _PvDBP_ orthologs were identified in the PvPAM assembly. When PvPAM PacBio reads were mapped against the PvPAM genome, no increase in _PvDBP_ coverage (indicative of a duplication) was observed either (Supplementary Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)).

### PvPAM drug resistance-associated genes

Although drug resistance-associated mutations remain largely elusive in _P. vivax_, antifolate-resistance SNPs have been described for _dhps_ and _dhfr_ [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR35 "Noviyanti R, Miotto O, Barry A, Marfurt J, Siegel S, Thuy-Nhien N, Quang HH, Anggraeni ND, Laihad F, Liu Y, et al. Implementing parasite genotyping into national surveillance frameworks: feedback from control programmes and researchers in the Asia–Pacific region. Malar J. 2020;19(1):271.")]. Antifolates are no longer recommended as a treatment in Peru, but the DHPS A383G and DHFR S58R and S117N resistance mutations are still highly prevalent in recently collected Peruvian samples [[36](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR36 "Flannery EL, Wang T, Akbari A, Corey VC, Gunawan F, Bright AT, Abraham M, Sanchez JF, Santolalla ML, Baldeviano GC, et al. Next-generation sequencing of Plasmodium vivax patient samples shows evidence of direct evolution in drug-resistance genes. ACS Infect Dis. 2015;1(8):367–79."),[37](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR37 "Villena FE, Sanchez JF, Nolasco O, Braga G, Ricopa L, Barazorda K, Salas CJ, Lucas C, Lizewski SE, Joya CA, et al. Drug resistance and population structure of Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax in the peruvian Amazon. Sci Rep. 2022;12(1):16474."),[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR38 "Kattenberg JH, Nguyen HV, Nguyen HL, Sauve E, Nguyen NTH, Chopo-Pizarro A, Trimarsanto H, Monsieurs P, Guetens P, Nguyen XX et al. Novel highly-multiplexed AmpliSeq targeted assay for Plasmodium vivax genetic surveillance use cases at multiple geographical scales. Front Cell Infect Microbiol 2022:1154.")]. As expected, these mutations are also present in the PvPAM genome. The PvP01 reference contains the same antifolate-resistance mutations as PvPAM, while PvW1 possesses a different combination of antifolate resistance SNPs (Supplementary Table[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)). Although the PvSalI genome is geographically the closest to PvPAM, PvSalI is still fully sensitive to antifolate drugs (Supplementary Table[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)), as it was collected almost 20 years before the first resistant cases were described [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR6 "Collins WE, Contacos PG, Krotoski WA, Howard WA. Transmission of four central american strains of Plasmodium vivax from monkey to man. J Parasitol. 1972;58(2):332–5."), [39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR39 "Rieckmann K, Davis D, Hutton D. Plasmodium vivax resistance to chloroquine? The Lancet. 1989;334(8673):1183–4.")]. Overall, the PvPAM _dhps_ and _dhfr_ genes align well to their PvSalI, PvP01 and PvW1 homologs (≥ 98.3% and ≥ 99.8% sequence identity, respectively), except for an in-frame increase of tandem repeats upstream of the final _dhps_ intron in PvPAM (Supplementary Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)A,B). Alignments of the chloroquine resistance-associated genes _mdr1_ and _crt_ [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR35 "Noviyanti R, Miotto O, Barry A, Marfurt J, Siegel S, Thuy-Nhien N, Quang HH, Anggraeni ND, Laihad F, Liu Y, et al. Implementing parasite genotyping into national surveillance frameworks: feedback from control programmes and researchers in the Asia–Pacific region. Malar J. 2020;19(1):271.")] of PvPAM, PvSalI, PvP01 and PvW1 show close similarities. PvPAM _mdr1_ has 99.9% sequence identity to the _mdr1_ genes in the 3 other reference genomes (Supplementary Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)C). PvPAM _crt_ showed a lower sequence identity of 96.8-99.2% to the _crt_ sequence in the other reference genomes, due to PvPAM indels in introns 5, 9 and 12 that are caused by variations in tandem repeats (Supplementary Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)D).

Gene duplications have been associated with antimalarial resistance as well, and the PvPAM PacBio reads were mapped to the PvPAM reference genome to check for increased coverage indicative of a potential duplication. In addition, a search for new orthology group members of resistance-associated genes was done. In South America, duplications of _crt_ (potential chloroquine resistance), _dhfr_ and _dhfs_ (potential antifolate resistance), and _mrp1_ (potential atovaquone resistance) have been described [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR36 "Flannery EL, Wang T, Akbari A, Corey VC, Gunawan F, Bright AT, Abraham M, Sanchez JF, Santolalla ML, Baldeviano GC, et al. Next-generation sequencing of Plasmodium vivax patient samples shows evidence of direct evolution in drug-resistance genes. ACS Infect Dis. 2015;1(8):367–79."), [40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR40 "Silva SR, Almeida ACG, da Silva GAV, Ramasawmy R, Lopes SCP, Siqueira AM, Costa GL, Sousa TN, Vieira JLF, Lacerda MVG, et al. Chloroquine resistance is associated to multi-copy pvcrt-o gene in Plasmodium vivax malaria in the brazilian Amazon. Malar J. 2018;17(1):267.")], but were not observed in PvPAM (Supplementary Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)). Mefloquine resistance-associated _mdr1_ gene duplications have mainly been observed in Southeast Asia [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR24 "Auburn S, Böhme U, Steinbiss S, Trimarsanto H, Hostetler J, Sanders M, Gao Q, Nosten F, Newbold CI, Berriman M et al. A new Plasmodium vivax reference sequence with improved assembly of the subtelomeres reveals an abundance of pir genes. Wellcome open Research 2016, 1(4)."), [41](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR41 "Costa GL, Amaral LC, Fontes CJF, Carvalho LH, de Brito CFA, de Sousa TN. Assessment of copy number variation in genes related to drug resistance in Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum isolates from the brazilian Amazon and a systematic review of the literature. Malar J. 2017;16(1):152."),[42](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR42 "Imwong M, Pukrittayakamee S, Pongtavornpinyo W, Nakeesathit S, Nair S, Newton P, Nosten F, Anderson TJ, Dondorp A, Day NP, et al. Gene amplification of the multidrug resistance 1 gene of Plasmodium vivax isolates from Thailand, Laos, and Myanmar. Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 2008;52(7):2657–9."),[43](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR43 "Lin JT, Patel JC, Kharabora O, Sattabongkot J, Muth S, Ubalee R, Schuster AL, Rogers WO, Wongsrichanalai C, Juliano JJ. Am J Trop Med Hyg. 2013;88(6):1116–23."),[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR44 "Suwanarusk R, Chavchich M, Russell B, Jaidee A, Chalfein F, Barends M, Prasetyorini B, Kenangalem E, Piera K, Lek-Uthai U, et al. Amplification of pvmdr1 associated with multidrug-resistant Plasmodium vivax. J Infect Dis. 2008;198(10):1558–64.")], and were not found in the Peruvian PvPAM genome (Supplementary Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)).

### South American samples mapped to PvPAM show more mapped reads and less read truncation

To investigate the difference in number of mapping reads between PvPAM, PvP01 and PvW1 as reference genome for South American WGS samples, WGS Illumina reads from 354 publicly available South American isolates and 63 non-South American isolates coming from Africa (N = 18) and Asia (N = 45), were mapped to the PvPAM, PvP01 and PvW1 reference genomes (overview of accession numbers and country of origin in Supplementary File [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)).

When South American WGS reads are mapped to each of the three reference genomes, differences in the number of mapped reads are small. 0.02-0.09% more reads align to PvPAM than to PvW1 or PvP01 (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig2)A; Wilcox _p_< 0.01 and < 0.0001 respectively). Additionally, 0.70% more non-South American reads are mapped to PvPAM than to PvP01 (Wilcox _p_< 0.0001), but there is no difference in the number of mapped reads between PvPAM and PvW1 (Wilcox _p_ non-significant; NS) (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig2)A). The reference genome’s effect on read alignment becomes more apparent when chimaeric (truncated) reads are analysed separately. Mapping of South American reads to PvPAM results in 13.94-41.77% less chimaeric reads compared to mapping to PvW1 or PvP01 (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig2)B; Wilcox _p_< 0.0001 for both). This indicates a higher structural similarity between South American isolates and PvPAM than with other reference genomes. Indeed, when reads from non-South American samples are mapped to the 3 reference genomes, the number of chimaeric reads is comparable between PvPAM and PvP01 (Wilcox _p_ NS), and 0.24% lower in PvW1 (Wilcox _p_< 0.05). This is in line with expectations, since 45 out of the 63 non-South American isolates are of Asian origin, and PvW1 originates from a Thai isolate that was sequenced with PacBio (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig2)B).

### PvPAM better reflects the South American variants

Since the PvPAM reference is derived from a Peruvian isolate, it likely resembles other South American isolates. Therefore, it is hypothesised that South American reads will contain fewer variants (SNPs, indels) when they are mapped to the PvPAM genome in comparison to PvP01 (Papua Indonesia) and PvW1 (Thailand). To investigate this, 354 publicly available Illumina WGS reads from South American samples (Peru, Brazil and Colombia; no other South American countries with > 10 WGS isolates were found in our public data search) were mapped to the PvPAM, PvP01 and PvW1 reference genomes and variant called. The same was done for 63 Illumina WGS samples from Africa (Eritrea, Ethiopia, Sudan, Uganda), South Asia (Afghanistan, India, Pakistan) and Southeast Asia (Cambodia, Malaysia, Myanmar, Papua New Guinea, Thailand, Vietnam). Since PvPAM has a slightly longer subtelomeric genome than PvP01 and PvW1 (9.4 Mb vs. 9.0 Mb) and since subtelomeric and core regions of the genome typically exhibit a different pattern of variant density (Supplementary Fig.[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)), variants of the core and subtelomeric genome were analysed separately.

When WGS reads from South American samples are mapped to the PvPAM genome, the number of variants in the core genome is significantly lower in comparison to PvP01 or PvW1 (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab2), Supplementary Fig.[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)A,C). Interestingly, alignment of non-South American reads to the PvPAM genome still results in less core genome variants than when PvP01 is used as reference, but more core genome variants than with PvW1 as reference (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab2), Supplementary Fig.[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)A,C). When the non-South American samples are divided into specific geographical regions, it becomes clear that reads from African and South Asian samples still contain the least core genome SNPs when mapped to PvPAM. Reads from Southeast Asian samples on the other hand, contain less core genome SNPs when mapped to PvP01 or PvW1 in comparison to PvPAM (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab2), Supplementary Fig.[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)B). When indels are assessed, African reads still contain the least indels when mapped to PvPAM, but both South Asian as Southeast Asian reads now have the least indels when aligned to PvW1. In each case though, the use of PvP01 results in the highest number of indels, highlighting the advantage of structurally more correct PacBio references (PvW1, PvPAM) in the context of indels (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab2), Supplementary Fig.[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)D). Overall, PvPAM is the most suited reference genome for use with South American and African WGS reads to investigate core genome variants, while PvW1 or PvP01 are a better choice for Southeast Asian reads. Both PvW1 and PvPAM are suited for South Asian reads, depending on whether core genome indels or SNPs are the main interest.

In the subtelomeric genome, reads from South American samples again show lower numbers of variants when mapped to PvPAM in comparison to the other 2 genomes (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab2), Supplementary Fig.[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)A-D). Reads from non-South American samples, however, now also show less subtelomeric variants when mapped to PvPAM than when mapped to PvP01 or PvW1 (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab2), Supplementary Fig.[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)A,C), and this is true for all the different geographical regions assessed (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab2), Supplementary Fig.[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)B,D). This shows that the PvPAM subtelomeres are more similar to the subtelomeric regions of isolates from all continents than the PvP01 or PvW1 subtelomeres, although the PvPAM subtelomeres still resemble the South American subtelomeres the most (largest decrease in median number of variants – Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab2)).

It can be concluded that the PvPAM reference reflects South American variants the best, and therefore, the generated vcf file containing variants of South American reads mapped to the PvPAM reference genome, can be of use for future research (available on the European Variation Archive (EVA)).
