## Discussion

This study presents the first high-quality South American _P. vivax_ reference genome, named PvPAM. Although South American _P. vivax_ isolates are genetically distinct from the other continents [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR12 "Benavente ED, Manko E, Phelan J, Campos M, Nolder D, Fernandez D, Velez-Tobon G, Castaño AT, Dombrowski JG, Marinho CRF, et al. Distinctive genetic structure and selection patterns in Plasmodium vivax from South Asia and East Africa. Nat Commun. 2021;12(1):3160.")] and are the predominant cause of malaria in South America [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR1 "WHO. World malaria report. In. Geneva: WHO; 2021.")], no qualitative South American _P. vivax_ reference genome existed until now. When compared to PvW1 and PvP01, PvPAM is the best suited reference genome for alignment of South American WGS reads. PvPAM was derived from a monoclonal _P. vivax_ malaria patient from the Peruvian Amazon, and the isolate did not undergo culture adaptation prior to sequencing. Only 9 ng of DNA extracted from 100 µl of leukocyte depleted RBCs (1% parasitaemia) was used for PacBio sequencing, in contrast to the 107 ng obtained from controlled human infections for the construction of the PvW1 PacBio reference genome [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465.")].

To assess the benefit of using a South American reference for read alignment of South American samples, PvPAM was compared to PvW1 and PvP01, the two other high-quality reference genomes existing for _P. vivax_. A small but significantly higher number of South American reads mapped to PvPAM in comparison to these other two references. More importantly, 14% and 42% less truncated reads were found compared to PvW1 and PvP01, respectively. For non-South-American samples, alignment to PvW1 and PvPAM resulted in a similarly high number of mapped reads, but use of the PacBio-based Thai PvW1 reference resulted in less truncated reads. Since read truncation is typically due to large structural variants (e.g. indels > 50 bp, translocations, inversions, copy number variations), this points towards continent-specific structural differences between the used reference genomes. In terms of number of mapped and truncated reads, PvPAM is well suited as a reference genome for South American WGS data, and is competitive with PvP01 and PvW1 for general use with WGS data from other continents.

The advantage of using a reference genome that is closely related to the genome of the sequenced isolate was further demonstrated by investigating the number of core genome variants. Alignment of South American WGS reads to the PvPAM reference showed the lowest number of core genome variants, indicating that South American samples resemble PvPAM most closely. Similarly, PvW1, originating from a Thai isolate, is the best reference to minimize the number of core genome variants in Southeast Asian samples. Alignment of African WGS reads to PvPAM still resulted in the lowest number of core genome variants, while alignment of South Asian reads to PvPAM and PvW1 produced the lowest number of core genome SNPs and indels, respectively. These findings mirror phylogenetic trees in which South American isolates are genetically most distinct from Southeast Asian isolates, but more similar to African and, to a lesser extent, South Asian isolates [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR12 "Benavente ED, Manko E, Phelan J, Campos M, Nolder D, Fernandez D, Velez-Tobon G, Castaño AT, Dombrowski JG, Marinho CRF, et al. Distinctive genetic structure and selection patterns in Plasmodium vivax from South Asia and East Africa. Nat Commun. 2021;12(1):3160.")].

Alignment of WGS reads to PvPAM always resulted in the lowest number of subtelomeric variants, regardless of the sample’s country of origin. Interestingly, even Southeast Asian samples showed less subtelomeric variants when mapped to PvPAM compared to the Thai and Pacbio-based PvW1. However, _Plasmodium_ subtelomeric regions remain largely elusive, and the extent to which the subtelomeric sequences vary between isolates and show geographical clustering is still uncertain. The subtelomeric regions of _P. falciparum_ have been shown to vary in length across isolates [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR45 "Otto TD, Böhme U, Sanders M, Reid A, Bruske EI, Duffy CW, Bull PC, Pearson RD, Abdi A, Dimonte S, et al. Long read assemblies of geographically dispersed Plasmodium falciparum isolates reveal highly structured subtelomeres. Wellcome Open Research. 2018;3:52.")], and similarly, PvPAM has longer subtelomeric regions than PvP01 or PvW1. The longer subtelomeres of PvPAM contain unique regions that are not present in either PvP01 or PvW1, which might result in a subtelomeric backbone that is better suited to align samples from all continents against. This could improve accuracy of read mapping and thus lead to lower variant densities.

The high-quality and longer subtelomeric regions of the PvPAM genome provide new insights into the subtelomeric gene families and their diversity. A comparison of _vir_ genes between PvP01 and PvPAM reveals that both have a high number of unique functional _vir_ genes that are absent in the other genome (723 and 605, respectively). It is possible that this high amount of uniquely identified _vir_ genes are of the same origin as the _vir_ genes found in PvP01, but that differences introduced by subtelomeric recombination caused the Companion annotation tool to identify many _vir_ genes as novel. This could be due to geographical differences between PvP01 and PvPAM, but it is also possible that there is an inherent variability in _vir_ genes, even across isolates from the same region. Other subtelomeric gene families did not show a gain or loss of gene members in PvPAM and appear to be more stable than the _vir_ family. However, more _P. vivax_ assemblies with high-quality subtelomeres are needed to study variation of _vir_ genes and other subtelomeric multigene families in depth. Some subtelomeric genes, such as the _PvTRAg25_-_PvTRAg33_ cluster, could for the first time be located to a chromosome. On the other hand, 12 subtelomeric PvPAM contigs could not be assigned to any chromosome based on PvP01 or PvW1 sequence similarity.

In this study, the core genome of PvPAM as well as PvP01 and PvW1 was defined based on GC-content and pairwise alignment between these three genomes. Although no standard definition is available for subtelomeric-core genome boundaries, GC-content has been used earlier as a marker for _P. vivax_ subtelomeres [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR4 "Carlton JM, Adams JH, Silva JC, Bidwell SL, Lorenzi H, Caler E, Crabtree J, Angiuoli SV, Merino EF, Amedeo P, et al. Comparative genomics of the neglected human malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. Nature. 2008;455(7214):757–63.")]. The provided core genome regions could be further refined by comparing positionally conserved genes across different _P. vivax_ isolates, as was done for _P. falciparum_ isolates [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR45 "Otto TD, Böhme U, Sanders M, Reid A, Bruske EI, Duffy CW, Bull PC, Pearson RD, Abdi A, Dimonte S, et al. Long read assemblies of geographically dispersed Plasmodium falciparum isolates reveal highly structured subtelomeres. Wellcome Open Research. 2018;3:52.")]. This, again, would require multiple high-quality _P. vivax_ subtelomere assemblies that are currently not available. However, the here used combination of long-read sequencing and a low-input material approach, might facilitate assembly of _P. vivax_ field isolates from blood volumes as small as a finger prick. In addition, Oxford Nanopore’s portable sequencer could become a quick and easy to use alternative for PacBio sequencing [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR46 "De Meulenaere K, Cuypers WL, Rosanas-Urgell A, Laukens K, Cuypers B. Selective whole-genome sequencing of Plasmodium parasites directly from blood samples by Nanopore adaptive sampling. bioRxiv. 2022. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.1111.1129.518068
                  
                .")], given further improvements in accuracy and DNA input requirements.

Finally, genome annotation was performed using the Companion annotation tool [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR47 "Steinbiss S, Silva-Franco F, Brunk B, Foth B, Hertz-Fowler C, Berriman M, Otto TD. Companion: a web server for annotation and analysis of parasite genomes. Nucleic Acids Res. 2016;44(W1):W29–W34.")], which provides an initial automatic annotation by transferring PvP01 annotations and conducting ab initio gene identification. However, due to limitations in the current version of this tool, we observed some missing genes in the mitochondrial and apicoplast genome of PvPAM compared to PvP01. Additional manual curation and an improved future version of the Companion tool will further enhance the PvPAM annotation. The PvPAM genome and new annotation releases will be made available on PlasmoDB.

## Conclusions

In summary, the PvPAM reference genome is the best choice to align South American WGS data to, highlighting the importance of using a continent-specific reference. Furthermore, it performed well for African and, to a lesser extent, South Asian WGS data. When studying subtelomeric regions, PvPAM proved to be the most suited reference genome, regardless of the sample’s continent of origin. Overall, the PvPAM reference genome will improve the quality of genomic analyses conducted on South American samples or subtelomeric genomes.

## Methods

### Collection and processing of _P. vivax_ patient blood samples

_P. vivax–_ infected blood was collected in 2019 from adult patients (≥ 18 years) with acute _P. vivax_ infection from the Peruvian city of Iquitos and neighbouring communities. All _P. vivax_ cases were diagnosed by light microscopy. 10–20 mL blood samples were collected in lithium-heparin tubes from patients with single _P. vivax_ infections with parasite densities > 0.1% and gametocyte proportion < 50%.

Blood samples from patients with _P. vivax_ infection were processed within 6 h of collection. Leukocytes and platelets were depleted using cellulose columns [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR48 "Sriprawat K, Kaewpongsri S, Suwanarusk R, Leimanis ML, Phyo AP, Snounou G, Russell B, Renia L, Nosten F. Effective and cheap removal of leukocytes and platelets from Plasmodium vivax infected blood. Malar J. 2009;8(1):115.")]. Then, 100 µl of _P. vivax–_ infected RBCs were stored at 50% haematocrit for future short- and long-read whole genome sequencing (WGS). The remaining blood was used for other purposes.

### DNA extraction and size selection of Pv01-19

Out of the 22 collected samples, sample Pv01-19 contained the highest parasitaemia of 1.0% (approximately 90% ring stages), and was therefore selected for long and short-read WGS. DNA was extracted from the stored 100 µl leukocyte-depleted RBCs using the QIAamp DNA mini kit (Qiagen), following the manufacturer’s instructions. After elution in 50 µL AE buffer, 0.46 ng/µl DNA was obtained. Fragments < 3 kb were removed with Ampure PB beads (2.2 V of 40% beads), and DNA was eluted in 50 µl PacBio elution buffer, resulting in 0.21 ng/µl DNA. Input fragment target size for the PacBio ultralow input protocol is 8–10 kilobases (kb). Since the concentration of Pv01-19 was too low (< 1 ng/µl), no Fragment Analyzer (Agilent) profile could be made. However, Fragment Analyzer profiles of higher concentration samples that were similarly stored fell within the 8–10 kb range, which is why no further shearing was applied on the Pv01-19 DNA.

### PacBio sequencing of Pv01-19

9 ng of DNA was used for library preparation with the SMRTbell Express Template Prep Kit 2.0, following the ultralow input protocol (version 01, August 2020). This protocol includes a 13-cycle PCR step to amplify the low amount of input DNA, using reagents from the SMRTbell gDNA Sample Amplification Kit (master mixes A and B cover different GC compositions). For the mix A PCR, 3 additional cycles were done to increase the yield. The final library was size-selected for fragments > 6,800 bases with a BluePippin device (Sage Science), since the Fragment Analyzer profile showed a peak at 8,304 bases. After clean-up, a 14.3 ng/µl library was obtained, with a fragment length peak at 8,341 bases (Femto Pulse, Agilent). The Femto Pulse trace showed no signs of dimer or overamplification.

SMRTbell templates were annealed with Sequencing Primer v4 and bound to a polymerase using the Sequel II binding Kit 2.0. SMRT Link settings for sequencing were entered according to the ultralow input protocol (CCS mode, Iso-Seq Experiment enabled, Iso-Seq Version Express to enable ProNex Cleanup workflow, with ProNex cleanup of 50% anticipated). Next, the library was loaded onto an 8 M SMRT cell and sequenced on a Sequel II with 2 h pe-extension time and 30 h movie time (Earlham Institute, Norwich). 6.1 million continuous long reads (CLR) were generated, resulting in a total number of 497 billion sequenced bases.

### Illumina sequencing of Pv01-19

To be able to polish PacBio sequencing errors, 1 ng DNA of the Pv01-19 sample was sent for Illumina sequencing (GenoScreen, Lille). The library was prepared with the Nextera XT DNA Sample Prep Kit (Illumina) following the manufacturer’s protocol, and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform with 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads. 68.3 million raw reads were generated, resulting in 10.3 billion sequenced bases.

### Pre-processing of PacBio reads

Reads were pre-processed with the PacBio secondary analysis tools available on PacBio Bioconda ([https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/pbbioconda](https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/pbbioconda)). Raw CLR subreads were converted to HiFi circular consensus sequencing (CCS) reads with pbccs v6.0.0 (--hifi-kinetics). During this process, 43% of the reads were lost, mainly due to misalignment of subreads from the same CLR read. To retain the ‘pw’ tag necessary for future Arrow assembly polishing, the ccs-kinetics-bystrandify tool (v2.0.0) from pbbam was used. PCR-adapters were trimmed with lima (--same --ccs --min-score 80), during which 5.6% of the CCS reads were lost. Next, duplicate removal with pbmarkdup v1.0.2 (--rmdup) caused another 5.6% of trimmed CCS read loss. This resulted in a final number of 24.5 billion CCS bases, with an average read length of 10,564 bases. To remove human reads, reads were mapped to the human genome (GRCh38) with the minimap2 wrapper pbmm2 v1.8.0 (--preset CCS --sort --unmapped), after which the unmapped reads were selected with samtools view (-f 4). Human reads represented only 0.18% of all CCS trimmed and non-duplicate bases.

Presence of contaminating species was checked with a Kraken2 run (--confidence 0.1; v2.0.9-beta) [[49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR49 "Wood DE, Lu J, Langmead B. Improved metagenomic analysis with Kraken 2. Genome Biol. 2019;20(1):257.")], during which the pre-processed and human-filtered reads were taxonomically classified with the PlusPF (09/08/22) database. No contaminants were identified that represented ≥ 0.01% of the reads.

Next, the pre-processed reads were mapped to the PvP01 reference genome (PlasmoDB, v51) with pbmm2 v1.8.0 to estimate the depth and check the similarity with the PvP01 reference genome.

### Assembly of the PvPAM reference genome

The pre-processed PacBio reads were _de novo_ assembled into a draft genome with Canu v2.0 (-pacbio hifi) [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR50 "Nurk S, Walenz BP, Rhie A, Vollger MR, Logsdon GA, Grothe R, Miga KH, Eichler EE, Phillippy AM, Koren S. HiCanu: accurate assembly of segmental duplications, satellites, and allelic variants from high-fidelity long reads. Genome Res. 2020;30(9):1291–305.")]. Next, contigs were scaffolded onto the PvP01 (PlasmoDB, v51) and PvW1 (PlasmoDB, v60) chromosomes using RagTag v2.1.0 (scaffold command, no prior correction done to prevent loss of strain-specific information) [[51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR51 "Alonge M, Lebeigle L, Kirsche M, Aganezov S, Wang X, Lippman ZB, Schatz MC, Soyk S. Automated assembly scaffolding using RagTag elevates a new tomato system for high-throughput genome editing. Genome Biol. 2022;23:258.")], and additional verification with minimap2 (-ax map-pb). When a contig was scaffolded differently on PvP01 as compared to PvW1, it was manually checked to which chromosomal location the contig fit best or if it had to be removed from the scaffold due to low confidence. 12 contigs could not be scaffolded confidently to any chromosome and remained unassigned. No contigs were scaffolded to the mitochondrial chromosome, due to its small size of approx. 6 kb (smaller than mean read length). Therefore, CCS reads that aligned (pbmm2) to the PvP01 or PvW1 mitochondrial chromosome were selected, duplicate removed (pbmarkdup), and assembled separately with Canu. Duplicated regions (circular chromosome) were manually removed.

Gaps between contigs of the same scaffold were then manually patched based on the PvW1 and PvP01 reference genome, using Geneious Prime (2022 release). PvW1 was preferentially used for patching, except when the contig ends only aligned to PvP01 (only the case for one patch on chromosome 2). Dotplots were made to check for large duplications due to assembly errors or due the circular mitochondrial and apicoplast chromosomes, but none were observed.

The assembly was polished based on the pre-processed CCS reads with 3 Arrow iterations (GCpp v2.0.2, [https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/gcpp](https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/gcpp)), introducing 5,967 changes to the assembly. This was followed by three iterations of Pilon (v1.23) short read polishing, resulting in 970 more changes. For each round of Pilon polishing, Illumina reads were mapped to the assembly with bwa mem v0.7.17, sorted on coordinates (samtools sort), duplicate reads were removed with Picard’s MarkDuplicates v2.22.0 (REMOVE_DUPLICATES = true), and confidently mapped reads (mapping quality = 60, no secondary reads) were selected with samtools view (-q60 -F256). The latter is done to prevent the shorter Illumina reads from misaligning to repetitive regions and incorrect polishing.

Completeness of the assembly was checked with Busco v5.4.4 [[52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR52 "Manni M, Berkeley MR, Seppey M, Simão FA, Zdobnov EM. BUSCO update: novel and streamlined workflows along with broader and deeper phylogenetic coverage for scoring of eukaryotic, prokaryotic, and viral genomes. Mol Biol Evol. 2021;38(10):4647–54.")]. Number of single-copy, fragmented and missing BUSCO’s (Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs) are within the same range for PvPAM, PvP01 and PvW1 (Supplementary Table[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)).

Finally, the PvPAM assembly was annotated with Companion v1.0.2 [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR47 "Steinbiss S, Silva-Franco F, Brunk B, Foth B, Hertz-Fowler C, Berriman M, Otto TD. Companion: a web server for annotation and analysis of parasite genomes. Nucleic Acids Res. 2016;44(W1):W29–W34.")]. Contiguation was turned off, reference proteins were aligned to the target sequence, and RATT was used for gene transfer (on species level) from the PvP01 reference genome. For other parameters, default settings were used.

### Defining the subtelomeric-core genome boundaries

Boundaries between the core genome and subtelomeric regions were here defined based on GC content. GC content was calculated per 1 kb window (sliding at steps of 100 bases) with bedtools v2.29.2 (makewindows, nuc). In R v4.2.1, draft subtelomeric boundaries were defined from both sides of the chromosome as the first window of a 10 kb region (100 consecutive windows) for which GC rose consistently above 35%. These draft core genome regions were then extracted from the PvPAM assembly with samtools faidx. Per chromosome, the PvPAM draft core region was aligned to the corresponding PvP01 (PlasmoDB, v46) and PvW1 chromosomes with Progressive Mauve (default settings) in Geneious Prime [[53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR53 "Darling AE, Mau B, Perna NT. progressiveMauve: multiple genome alignment with gene gain, loss and rearrangement. PLoS ONE. 2010;5(6):e11147.")]. The part of the draft core region that aligned to the 2 other reference genomes was considered to be the final core genome region, and these regions are shown in Supplementary File [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM2).

Unassigned contigs were categorised as subtelomeric or core based on their GC content. If the GC content was below the mean GC content of the core and subtelomeric regions of the 14 chromosomes (as determined above), the contig was considered subtelomeric. This was the case for all contigs of PvPAM and PvW1, and for 207/226 contigs of PvP01 (Supplementary File [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM2)).

Raw reads were mapped to the human reference genome (GRCh38) with bwa mem v0.7.17 and coordinate sorted with samtools, after which the non-human reads that did not map as a pair were selected (samtools view -F 2) and converted to the fastq format again (samtools fastq). Those were then mapped to the PvPAM, PvP01 (version 46) or PvW1 reference genome with bwa mem, coordinate sorted, and duplicate marked with Picard MarkDuplicates v2.22.0. Per sample, the median alignment score was extracted using an awk loop, and number of primary and chimaeric reads were extracted with samtools view -c (-F 256 -F 2048 -F 1024 and -f 2048 -F 1024 respectively). The same was done on only the core genome of those same mapped files, as defined in previous section (Supplementary File [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM2)).

Next variants were called using the GATK (v4.1.4.1) HaplotypeCaller (-ERC GVCF), and resulting gvcf files samples were combined (GATK CombineGVCFs) and converted (GATK GenotypeGVCFs) to a South American and a non-South American vcf file. Each vcf was split into a SNP and indel vcf (GATK SelectVariants), after which filter fields were defined according to the GATK golden standard with VariantFiltration (for the SNP vcf: QD < 2.0, QUAL < 30.0, SOR > 3.0, FS > 60.0, MQ < 40.0, MQRankSum<-12.5, ReadPosRankSum<-8.0; for the indel vcf: QD < 2.0, QUAL < 30.0, FS > 200.0, ReadPosRankSum<-20.0). Only variants that passed the filters described and did not have > 50% of missing genotypes (bcftools view -i ‘F_MISSING < 0.5’) were retained in the vcf files. Variants were annotated with SnpEff v4.3t and the -stats summary was used to compare the variant rate per base, mean allele frequency and mean indel length between the three used reference genomes. This was repeated on the same vcf files for which first the core genome was extracted (core genome regions in Supplementary File [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM2)). Vcf files are made available under Study PRJEB60575 on the European Nucleotide Archive, and Supplementary File [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1) links the WGS samples names used in the vcf to their accession numbers.

### Multiplicity of infection (MOI) estimation of Pv01-19

To estimate the MOI of Pv01-19, its Illumina reads were mapped to PvP01 (PlasmoDB v46) with bwa mem v0.7.17 and coordinate sorted (samtools sort), and duplicate reads were flagged with Picard’s MarkDuplicates v2.22.0. The same was done for Illumina reads from 15 other Peruvian samples collected at the same location and in the same way (BioProject PRJNA853729) [[57](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR57 "De Meulenaere K, Prajapati SK, Villasis E, Cuypers B, Kattenberg JH, Kasian B, Laman M, Robinson LJ, Gamboa D, Laukens K, et al. Band 3–mediated Plasmodium vivax invasion is associated with transcriptional variation in PvTRAg genes. Front Cell Infect Microbiol. 2022;12:1011692.")], to provide samples for comparison to the MOI estimation tools. Pv01-19 was variant called together with the 15 other Peruvian samples following the same pipeline as described in previous section for the public data samples. Core and non-hypervariable regions as defined by Pearson et al. (2016) were extracted from the SNP vcf with bcftools tabix, after which estMOI v1.03 [[62](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR62 "Assefa SA, Preston MD, Campino S, Ocholla H, Sutherland CJ, Clark TG. estMOI: estimating multiplicity of infection using parasite deep sequencing data. Bioinformatics. 2014;30(9):1292–4.")] and the moimix R package [[63](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR63 "Lee S, Bahlo M. moimix: an R package for assessing clonality in high-throughput sequencing data. moimix: an R package for assessing clonality in high-throughput sequencing data 2016.")] were ran. Both tools estimated a MOI = 1 for Pv01-19.

### Statistical analysis

Non-parametrical paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were performed in R v4.2.1 [[64](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR64 "R Core Team. : R: A language and environment for statistical computing. In. Vienna, Austria: R Foundation for Statistical Computing; 2019.")].

## Data Availability

The annotated reference genome and raw PacBio and Illumina reads used for its construction are available under Study PRJEB59758 in de European Nucleotide Archive ([https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/)). Additionally, the reference genome (.fasta.gz) and annotation file (gff3 format) are made available in Supplementary Files [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM3) and [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM4), respectively. Newly generated WGS Illumina reads from Peruvian (N = 7) and Brazilian (N = 21) samples are made available under BioProjects PRJNA853729 and PRJNA934307 in the Sequence Read Archive, respectively ([https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra)). The variant files (.vcf) containing SNPs and indels of publicly available South American WGS Illumina data mapped to the PvPAM genome, are available under Study PRJEB60575 in the European Nucleotide Archive ([https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/)). Supplementary File [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1) links the sample names used in the vcf to their accession numbers.

## Abstract

### Background

_Plasmodium vivax_ is the second most important cause of human malaria worldwide, and accounts for the majority of malaria cases in South America. A high-quality reference genome exists for Papua Indonesia (PvP01) and Thailand (PvW1), but is lacking for South America. A reference genome specifically for South America would be beneficial though, as _P. vivax_ is a genetically diverse parasite with geographical clustering.

### Results

This study presents a new high-quality assembly of a South American _P. vivax_ isolate, referred to as PvPAM (_P. vivax_ Peruvian AMazon). The genome was obtained from a low input patient sample from the Peruvian Amazon and sequenced using PacBio technology, resulting in a highly complete assembly with 6497 functional genes. Telomeric ends were present in 17 out of 28 chromosomal ends, and additional (sub)telomeric regions are present in 12 unassigned contigs. A comparison of multigene families between PvPAM and the PvP01 genome revealed remarkable variation in _vir_ genes, and the presence of merozoite surface proteins (MSP) 3.6 and 3.7. Three _dhfr_ and _dhps_ drug resistance associated mutations are present in PvPAM, similar to those found in other Peruvian isolates. Mapping of publicly available South American whole genome sequencing (WGS) data to PvPAM resulted in significantly fewer variants and truncated reads compared to the use of PvP01 or PvW1 as reference genomes. To minimize the number of core genome variants in non-South American samples, PvW1 is most suited for Southeast Asian isolates, both PvPAM and PvW1 are suited for South Asian isolates, and PvPAM is recommended for African isolates. Interestingly, non-South American samples still contained the least subtelomeric variants when mapped to PvPAM, indicating high quality of the PvPAM subtelomeric regions.

### Conclusions

Our findings show that the PvPAM reference genome more accurately represents South American _P. vivax_ isolates in comparison to PvP01 and PvW1. In addition, PvPAM has a high level of completeness, and contains a similar number of annotated genes as PvP01 or PvW1. The PvPAM genome therefore will be a valuable resource to improve future genomic analyses on _P. vivax_ isolates from the South American continent.

## Background

_Plasmodium vivax_ is the second most common cause of malaria in humans after _P. falciparum_. _P. vivax_ is widespread outside of Africa, accounting there for one-third of the malaria infections [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR1 "WHO. World malaria report. In. Geneva: WHO; 2021.")]. Due to the absence of a continuous culturing system [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR2 "Bermúdez M, Moreno-Pérez DA, Arévalo-Pinzón G, Curtidor H, Patarroyo MA. Plasmodium vivax in vitro continuous culture: the spoke in the wheel. Malar J. 2018;17(301):1–12.")] and the former assumption that _P. vivax_ infections are benign [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR3 "Howes RE, Battle KE, Mendis KN, Smith DL, Cibulskis RE, Baird JK, Hay SI. Global epidemiology of Plasmodium vivax. Am J Trop Med Hyg. 2016;95(6 Suppl):15–34.")], _P. vivax_ research has been lagging behind that of _P. falciparum_. Only in 2008, the first _P. vivax_ reference genome, Salvador I, was assembled [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR4 "Carlton JM, Adams JH, Silva JC, Bidwell SL, Lorenzi H, Caler E, Crabtree J, Angiuoli SV, Merino EF, Amedeo P, et al. Comparative genomics of the neglected human malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. Nature. 2008;455(7214):757–63.")], while the _P. falciparum_ 3D7 reference genome was already published in 2002 [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR5 "Gardner MJ, Hall N, Fung E, White O, Berriman M, Hyman RW, Carlton JM, Pain A, Nelson KE, Bowman S, et al. Genome sequence of the human malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Nature. 2002;419(6906):498–511.")].

Hitherto, several _P. vivax_ genomes have been assembled for _P. vivax_. The Salvador I (PvSalI) genome was assembled from paired-read Sanger sequencing data, coming from an El Salvador isolate that was passaged in _Saimiri_ monkeys [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR4 "Carlton JM, Adams JH, Silva JC, Bidwell SL, Lorenzi H, Caler E, Crabtree J, Angiuoli SV, Merino EF, Amedeo P, et al. Comparative genomics of the neglected human malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. Nature. 2008;455(7214):757–63."), [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR6 "Collins WE, Contacos PG, Krotoski WA, Howard WA. Transmission of four central american strains of Plasmodium vivax from monkey to man. J Parasitol. 1972;58(2):332–5.")]. However, it contains > 2000 unassigned contigs that were not assigned to a chromosome, making it less suited for alignment of whole genome sequencing (WGS) data. Similarly, Illumina-based assemblies from four monkey-passaged isolates from Brazil, India, Mauritania and North Korea [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR7 "Neafsey DE, Galinsky K, Jiang RHY, Young L, Sykes SM, Saif S, Gujja S, Goldberg JM, Young S, Zeng Q, et al. The malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax exhibits greater genetic diversity than Plasmodium falciparum. Nat Genet. 2012;44(9):1046–50.")] and 1 Cambodian field isolate [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR8 "Hester J, Chan ER, Menard D, Mercereau-Puijalon O, Barnwell J, Zimmerman PA, Serre D. De novo assembly of a field isolate genome reveals novel Plasmodium vivax erythrocyte invasion genes. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2013;7(12):e2569.")] were highly fragmented, with > 1500 scaffolds. More recently, Auburn et al. (2016) released a high-quality reference genome from an Illumina-sequenced Papua Indonesian isolate (PvP01), along with two draft assemblies from Thailand (PvT01) and China (PvC01). Finally, a Thai isolate used in controlled human infections was long-read sequenced with PacBio, resulting in the high-quality PvW1 reference genome [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465.")].

South America is not yet represented by the existing high-quality reference genomes (PvP01, PvW1), although the majority of the malaria cases in this continent are _P. vivax_ [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR1 "WHO. World malaria report. In. Geneva: WHO; 2021.")]. Since _P. vivax_ is genetically more diverse than _P. falciparum_ [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR7 "Neafsey DE, Galinsky K, Jiang RHY, Young L, Sykes SM, Saif S, Gujja S, Goldberg JM, Young S, Zeng Q, et al. The malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax exhibits greater genetic diversity than Plasmodium falciparum. Nat Genet. 2012;44(9):1046–50."), [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR10 "Fola AA, Harrison GA, Hazairin MH, Barnadas C, Hetzel MW, Iga J, Siba PM, Mueller I, Barry AE. Higher complexity of infection and genetic diversity of Plasmodium vivax than Plasmodium falciparum across all malaria transmission zones of Papua New Guinea. Am J Trop Med Hyg. 2017;96(3):630–41."), [11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR11 "Hupalo DN, Luo Z, Melnikov A, Sutton PL, Rogov P, Escalante A, Vallejo AF, Herrera S, Arévalo-Herrera M, Fan Q, et al. Population genomics studies identify signatures of global dispersal and drug resistance in Plasmodium vivax. Nat Genet. 2016;48(8):953–8.")], there is a strong geographical differentiation between isolates from different continents [[11](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR11 "Hupalo DN, Luo Z, Melnikov A, Sutton PL, Rogov P, Escalante A, Vallejo AF, Herrera S, Arévalo-Herrera M, Fan Q, et al. Population genomics studies identify signatures of global dispersal and drug resistance in Plasmodium vivax. Nat Genet. 2016;48(8):953–8."),[12](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR12 "Benavente ED, Manko E, Phelan J, Campos M, Nolder D, Fernandez D, Velez-Tobon G, Castaño AT, Dombrowski JG, Marinho CRF, et al. Distinctive genetic structure and selection patterns in Plasmodium vivax from South Asia and East Africa. Nat Commun. 2021;12(1):3160."),[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR13 "Koepfli C, Rodrigues PT, Antao T, Orjuela-Sánchez P, Van den Eede P, Gamboa D, Van Hong N, Bendezu J, Erhart A, Barnadas C, et al. Plasmodium vivax diversity and population structure across four continents. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2015;9(6):e0003872.")]. The PvP01 and PvW1 assemblies originate from Papua Indonesia and Thailand, and isolates from these countries are genetically distant from the South American ones [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR12 "Benavente ED, Manko E, Phelan J, Campos M, Nolder D, Fernandez D, Velez-Tobon G, Castaño AT, Dombrowski JG, Marinho CRF, et al. Distinctive genetic structure and selection patterns in Plasmodium vivax from South Asia and East Africa. Nat Commun. 2021;12(1):3160.")]. Therefore, a new _P. vivax_ reference genome from South American origin could improve variant calling of South American isolates and provide more accurate information on indels (insertions and deletions) and large structural variants. Especially these large structural variants cannot be detected readily by aligning short-read sequences to a reference genome, which is why continent-specific reference genomes are expected to increase mapping quality and reveal new or missing genes. This will have a greater impact in the subtelomeric regions, which are highly dynamic with frequent duplication and recombination events [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR14 "Mok BW, Ribacke U, Sherwood E, Wahlgren M. A highly conserved segmental duplication in the subtelomeres of Plasmodium falciparum chromosomes varies in copy number. Malar J. 2008;7(1):1–9.")], and contain important multigene families involved in immune evasion and host-parasite interactions [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR4 "Carlton JM, Adams JH, Silva JC, Bidwell SL, Lorenzi H, Caler E, Crabtree J, Angiuoli SV, Merino EF, Amedeo P, et al. Comparative genomics of the neglected human malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. Nature. 2008;455(7214):757–63.")]. In addition, accurate reflection of the sample’s structural variants in the reference genome can help the assessment of RNA isoforms, which are known to be abundant in _P. vivax_ [[15](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR15 "Zhu L, Mok S, Imwong M, Jaidee A, Russell B, Nosten F, Day NP, White NJ, Preiser PR, Bozdech Z. New insights into the Plasmodium vivax transcriptome using RNA-Seq. Sci Rep. 2016;6(1):20498."),[16](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR16 "Kim A, Popovici J, Vantaux A, Samreth R, Bin S, Kim S, Roesch C, Liang L, Davies H, Felgner P, et al. Characterization of P. vivax blood stage transcriptomes from field isolates reveals similarities among infections and complex gene isoforms. Sci Rep. 2017;7(1):7761."),[17](https://bmcgenomics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR17 "Siegel SV, Chappell L, Hostetler JB, Amaratunga C, Suon S, Bohme U, Berriman M, Fairhurst RM, Rayner JC. Analysis of Plasmodium vivax schizont transcriptomes from field isolates reveals heterogeneity of expression of genes involved in host-parasite interactions. Sci Rep. 2020;10(1):16667."),[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR18 "Hazzard B, Sá JM, Ellis AC, Pascini TV, Amin S, Wellems TE, Serre D. Long read single cell RNA sequencing reveals the isoform diversity of Plasmodium vivax transcripts. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2022;16(12):e0010991.")].

Since _de novo_ assembly of a reference genome makes use of the overlaps between sequenced fragments (reads), longer reads improve confidence and quality of the assembly. In addition, long reads can better resolve repetitive or low-complexity regions often found in the subtelomeres. Short-read technologies like Illumina typically have read lengths of 50–300 bases, while Pacific Biosciences SMRT technology (PacBio) and Oxford Nanopore technology (ONT), the leading long-read sequencing technologies to date, readily exceed 10,000 bases. Therefore, PacBio and Nanopore are more suited for reference genome sequencing. At the moment of writing, PacBio sequencing has an accuracy of 99.8% [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR19 "Wenger AM, Peluso P, Rowell WJ, Chang P-C, Hall RJ, Concepcion GT, Ebler J, Fungtammasan A, Kolesnikov A, Olson ND, et al. Accurate circular consensus long-read sequencing improves variant detection and assembly of a human genome. Nat Biotechnol. 2019;37(10):1155–62.")], similar to what can be achieved with Illumina sequencing, and higher than the 99% that can be reached with the Nanopore R10.4 chemistry [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR20 "Sereika M, Kirkegaard RH, Karst SM, Michaelsen TY, Sørensen EA, Wollenberg RD, Albertsen M. Oxford Nanopore R10.4 long-read sequencing enables the generation of near-finished bacterial genomes from pure cultures and metagenomes without short-read or reference polishing. Nat Methods. 2022;19(7):823–6.")]. Due to PacBio’s use of circular consensus sequencing (a circular read is sequenced multiple times), random sequencing errors are largely removed [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR19 "Wenger AM, Peluso P, Rowell WJ, Chang P-C, Hall RJ, Concepcion GT, Ebler J, Fungtammasan A, Kolesnikov A, Olson ND, et al. Accurate circular consensus long-read sequencing improves variant detection and assembly of a human genome. Nat Biotechnol. 2019;37(10):1155–62.")]. Although a bias for indels at homopolymer regions remains [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR19 "Wenger AM, Peluso P, Rowell WJ, Chang P-C, Hall RJ, Concepcion GT, Ebler J, Fungtammasan A, Kolesnikov A, Olson ND, et al. Accurate circular consensus long-read sequencing improves variant detection and assembly of a human genome. Nat Biotechnol. 2019;37(10):1155–62."), [21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR21 "Karst SM, Ziels RM, Kirkegaard RH, Sørensen EA, McDonald D, Zhu Q, Knight R, Albertsen M. High-accuracy long-read amplicon sequences using unique molecular identifiers with Nanopore or PacBio sequencing. Nat Methods. 2021;18(2):165–9.")], it is the most robust long-read sequencing method to date, which was also used to construct the Thai PvW1 reference [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465.")]. The PvW1 sample was obtained from controlled human malaria infections, which allows extraction of a high amount of input DNA. However, low input protocols are becoming more common, and PacBio recently released their Ultra-Low DNA Input protocol (5–20 ng DNA) [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR22 "Ultra-Low DNA. Input Workflow for SMRT Sequencing [
                  https://www.pacb.com/plant-animal-biology/introducing-the-ultra-low-input-protocol-for-smrt-sequencing/
                  
                ].")]. This provides opportunities to long-read sequence _P. vivax_ DNA from low blood volume and/or low parasitaemia patient samples, which is common in natural human infections.

In this study, a leukocyte-depleted blood sample from a _P. vivax_ patient from the Peruvian Amazon was sequenced with PacBio using the Ultra-Low DNA Input protocol, allowing the assembly of a new and high-quality South American reference genome named PvPAM (_P. vivax_ Peruvian AMazon). The PvPAM chromosomes have a high level of completeness (telomeric repeats in 17/28 chromosomal ends), although 12 unassigned contigs remain. A variant analysis of publicly available WGS data shows that the PvPAM core genome represents South American and African isolates better than the PvP01 and PvW1 reference genomes. In the subtelomeric regions, the use of PvPAM as a reference genome resulted in a significantly lower number of variants for WGS data from all continents, outperforming PvP01 and PvW1.

## Results

### Construction of a high-quality reference genome from a low-input _P. vivax_ patient DNA sample

A new reference genome was constructed from a monoclonal _P. vivax_ patient sample originating from the Peruvian Amazon basin (Iquitos), which we named PvPAM (_P. vivax_ Peruvian AMazon). Although the input sample contained a very low amount of parasite DNA (9 ng), the PacBio Ultra-Low Input protocol for library preparation allowed to sequence the _P. vivax_ genome in high depth and enabled to build a high-quality reference genome for the South American Amazon region.

497 billion raw continuous long read (CLR) bases were sequenced, and after pre-processing, 24.5 billion high fidelity circular consensus sequencing (CCS) read bases were left, with reads being 10,670 bases long on average. When mapped to the PvP01 reference genome, this resulted in an average sequencing depth of 821x. This is well above the recommended 15x depth for assembly of a haploid genome [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR23 "PacBio. Application note - considerations for using the low and ultra-low DNA input workflows for whole genome sequencing V2. In.; 2020: 12.")], but due to the repetitive and AT-rich subtelomeric regions, higher depths are necessary to fully assemble the eukaryotic _P. vivax_ genome.

Genome assembly and subsequent scaffolding resulted in 14 chromosomes, of which 4 were completely assembled, while the other 10 were scaffolds consisting of 2–4 contigs. The gaps between those contigs were patched based on the PvP01 and PvW1 reference genomes [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465."), [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR24 "Auburn S, Böhme U, Steinbiss S, Trimarsanto H, Hostetler J, Sanders M, Gao Q, Nosten F, Newbold CI, Berriman M et al. A new Plasmodium vivax reference sequence with improved assembly of the subtelomeres reveals an abundance of pir genes. Wellcome open Research 2016, 1(4).")]. The patches had a median length of 388 bases (range 41-2592 bases) (Supplementary Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)), which indicates that the initial PvPAM assembly was of good quality and only few bases were uncovered. Further polishing of the genome with Illumina reads, obtained in parallel from the PvPAM isolate, introduced some PvPAM-specific changes in the patched regions. In addition to the 14 chromosomes, 12 contigs could not be uniquely assigned to any chromosome, although they were identified as subtelomeric based on their low GC content (< 25%) and presence of _vir_ (variant interspersed repeat) genes.

PvPAM chromosome-completeness was assessed by the presence of telomeric CCCT(A/G)AA repeats [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR25 "Ponzi M, Pace T, Dore E, Frontali C. Identification of a telomeric DNA sequence in Plasmodium berghei. EMBO J. 1985;4(11):2991–5."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR26 "Vernick KD, McCutchan TF. Sequence and structure of a Plasmodium falciparum telomere. Mol Biochem Parasitol. 1988;28(2):85–94.")], which indicate that the chromosome was fully assembled up to the 5’ or 3’ end. Telomeric repeats were only observed at one chromosomal end in PvP01, while they are present in 17/28 chromosomal ends in the PvPAM, indicating a higher number of completely assembled chromosomes (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)). Eight additional telomeric repeat sequences could be found in the 12 unassigned and subtelomeric PvPAM contigs.

### Structural comparison of PvPAM to the PvP01 and PvW1 reference genomes

PvPAM was compared on a structural and annotation level to the two highest quality _P. vivax_ reference genomes existing to date: PvP01 [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR24 "Auburn S, Böhme U, Steinbiss S, Trimarsanto H, Hostetler J, Sanders M, Gao Q, Nosten F, Newbold CI, Berriman M et al. A new Plasmodium vivax reference sequence with improved assembly of the subtelomeres reveals an abundance of pir genes. Wellcome open Research 2016, 1(4).")] and the PacBio-based PvW1 [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR9 "Minassian AM, Themistocleous Y, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Kemp A, Quinkert D, Nielsen CM, Edwards NJ, Rawlinson TA, Ramos Lopez F, et al. Controlled human malaria infection with a clone of Plasmodium vivax with high quality genome assembly. JCI Insight. 2021;6(23):e152465.")]. These three reference genomes have overall similar genome sizes (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab1)). However, whole genome alignments of the reference genomes reveal that most PvPAM chromosomes contain longer subtelomeric regions than their PvP01 counterparts (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)A). This is because large parts of the PvP01 subtelomeric regions are divided over many short contigs that are not assigned to any chromosome, while the PvPAM reference genome is less fragmented. The subtelomeric regions of the PvW1 chromosomes are overall of similar length as in PvPAM (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab1)), but at the chromosome level, the subtelomeres often have different lengths or do not fully align (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)B). We determined core genome boundaries based on GC-content and sequence identity between PvPAM, PvP01 and PvW1. These borders show that the PvW1 and PvPAM chromosomes possess longer subtelomeric regions than the PvP01 chromosomes, due to higher contiguity in PacBio-based genomes (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab1)).

The PvPAM genome contains 6497 functional genes (i.e., genes not annotated as a pseudogene), a higher number than found in PvW1, but still less than in PvP01 (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Tab1)). Out of the 6497 functional genes, 1109 are not present in PvP01. Of those, 487 genes cannot be linked to any PvP01 gene through orthology, and are therefore new in the PvPAM reference genome (Supplementary Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#MOESM1)). The number of PvPAM pseudogenes is higher than what was observed for PvP01 (4.7% vs. 2.7% of all genes). Pseudogenes are mainly located in the subtelomeres (89% of PvPAM and 95% of PvP01 pseudogenes), due to the dynamic nature of this region [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR14 "Mok BW, Ribacke U, Sherwood E, Wahlgren M. A highly conserved segmental duplication in the subtelomeres of Plasmodium falciparum chromosomes varies in copy number. Malar J. 2008;7(1):1–9.")]. In the PvPAM mitochondrial and apicoplast genome, less functional genes were annotated in comparison to PvP01. In the apicoplast, this is partly due to its shorter length in PvPAM (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)D). However, the PvPAM apicoplast and mitochondrial genome are highly similar to PvP01 (Figs.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#Fig1)C-D and 89.1% and 99.9% pairwise identity with MUSCLE, respectively), and missing gene annotations are attributed to a limitation of the Companion annotation tool.

### PvPAM multigene families in subtelomeric or internally variable regions

Multigene families located at the subtelomeres or internally variable regions often play an important role in host-parasite interactions, immune response and pathogenicity, and can vary in (pseudo)gene number across isolates due to the dynamic nature of subtelomeres [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-023-09707-5#ref-CR4 "Carlton JM, Adams JH, Silva JC, Bidwell SL, Lorenzi H, Caler E, Crabtree J, Angiuoli SV, Merino EF, Amedeo P, et al. Comparative genomics of the neglected human malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. Nature. 2008;455(7214):757–63.")]. In particular, the _P. vivax_ variant genes (_vir_) are known to be involved in immune invasion, and the _P. vivax_ tryptophan-rich antigens (PvTRAg), _P. vivax_ reticulocyte binding proteins (PvRBP) and _P. vivax_ merozoite surface proteins (MSP) take part in invasion or red blood cell (RBC) binding.

In the PvPAM genome, 975 + 99 _vir_ genes (functional genes + pseudogenes) were found, which is less than the 1093 + 116 in PvP01 and 1145 functional _vir_ genes in PvW1. Remarkably, out of these 975 functional _vir_ genes identified in PvPAM, only 370 have been transferred from the PvP01 reference genome through sequence similarity. The remaining 605 _vir_ genes are newly predicted in PvPAM.

All 40 _PvTRAg_ genes present in PvP01 were also found in PvPAM. ## Gene Counts Across High-Quality *P. vivax* Reference Genomes

Recent long-read and highly contiguous genome assemblies have fundamentally changed our understanding of the scale of subtelomeric multigene families. The table below summarizes the number of functional genes annotated for the PIR (VIR) and PHIST families in the three most prominent modern reference assemblies.

| Reference Genome | Geography / Origin | Technology | PIR / VIR count | PHIST count |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **PvP01** (GCA_900093555.2) | Papua, Indonesia | Illumina (deep) | ~1,219 | 39 |
| **PvW1** (GCA_914969965.1) | Thailand | Hybrid (PacBio + Illumina) | 1,145 | ~39 |
| **PvPAM** (GCA_949152365.1) | Peruvian Amazon | PacBio | 975 | ~39 |

*Note: The older, highly fragmented Salvador-I (Sanger sequencing) reference only captured ~346 VIR genes. The counts above represent fully annotated, functional genes (excluding pseudogenes, which add an additional ~100 copies per assembly). Notably, in PvPAM, over 600 of its VIR genes share no direct orthology with PvP01, highlighting the massive geographic diversity of these subtelomeric expansions.*

### PHIST (Plasmodium Helical Interspersed Subtelomeric)
* **Copy Number:** This family exhibits significant lineage-specific expansion in human and primate malarias compared to rodent models. There are roughly **39 *phist* genes in *P. vivax*** and **~65-72 copies in *P. falciparum***. By stark contrast, rodent malaria models (like *P. berghei* or *P. yoelii*) possess severely contracted families, containing only 1 to 3 copies.
* **Gene Structure:** Like many *Plasmodium* exported protein families, *phist* genes are primarily located in the hyper-recombinogenic subtelomeric regions and typically share a conserved **two-exon structure**:
  * **Exon 1:** A short sequence that encodes a hydrophobic signal peptide for initial entry into the parasite's secretory pathway.
  * **Exon 2:** A much larger exon that usually begins with a *Plasmodium* Export Element (PEXEL) motif—a targeting signal to export the protein into the host erythrocyte—followed by the sequence encoding the defining PHIST domain and the rest of the protein.
* **Protein Structure:** The defining feature of PHIST proteins is the **PHIST domain**, a conserved region of approximately 150 amino acids. Structurally, this domain consists of four consecutive alpha-helices with conserved aromatic residues. The domain itself does not possess known enzymatic activity; rather, it acts as a critical protein-protein interaction module.
* **Function:** PHIST proteins are essentially the "scaffold builders" and "anchors" inside the infected human red blood cell. Once exported, they localize to the host cell cytoskeleton or to membranous structures called Maurer's clefts. Their primary function is to remodel the host cell. Crucially, they bind to major virulence factors (like PfEMP1 in *P. falciparum* or its equivalents) and anchor them securely to the red blood cell's cytoskeleton (specifically interacting with human host proteins like band 4.1R). Without PHIST proteins securely anchoring these surface antigens, the infected red blood cell cannot properly adhere to blood vessel walls, drastically reducing the parasite's virulence.

These counts are based on **PlasmoDB** annotations (and the primary publications that feed into it), rather than NCBI's automated RefSeq pipeline. 

Specifically, the comparative genomic study that assembled the **PvPAM** genome derived these counts by comparing their new assembly against **PvP01 (PlasmoDB version 51)** and **PvW1 (PlasmoDB version 60)**. 

The distinction is actually quite important for *Plasmodium*:
* **PlasmoDB (and the Sanger Institute's *Companion* pipeline):** These use highly specialized, manually curated algorithms designed specifically for *Plasmodium* to correctly identify PEXEL motifs, export signals, and complex subtelomeric repeat families like PIR and PHIST.
* **NCBI (RefSeq):** NCBI uses its generalized automated eukaryotic annotation pipeline (GNOMON). While excellent generally, it often struggles with the hyper-repetitive, AT-rich subtelomeres of *Plasmodium*. It frequently merges adjacent *vir* genes, improperly fragments them, or misclassifies them as pseudogenes, leading to different (and usually less accurate) gene counts for these specific families.

**Analyzing Annotation Consistency**

I've been digging into the *Plasmodium vivax* assemblies, noticing a significant bias in the RefSeq and GenBank annotations of subtelomeric genes. The original submission approach seems to heavily influence these automated annotations, making the reported gene counts in publications very inconsistent, and strongly dependant on the submission itself.


**Clarifying Annotation Discrepancies**

I've realized that NCBI annotations for subtelomeric genes are essentially the authors' original submissions, especially for GenBank assemblies (GCA_). This directly influences the reported gene counts. The RefSeq assembly (GCF_) for Salvador I has "Full annotation," but others only have the submitted annotations, highlighting the inconsistency. I'm focusing on retrieving gene counts directly from NCBI Datasets/Assembly to quantify the differences.

content.text:
I checked the NCBI assembly records for these three genomes, and there is an important detail about how *Plasmodium* annotations are handled:

**The counts on NCBI are identical to the PlasmoDB counts.** 

Here is why: 
None of these three modern long-read assemblies (PvP01, PvW1, PvPAM) have been processed through NCBI's automated Eukaryotic Genome Annotation Pipeline (RefSeq). Instead, they are hosted as GenBank (`GCA_`) assemblies rather than RefSeq (`GCF_`) assemblies. 

Because of this, the annotations available on NCBI for these genomes are exactly the **author-submitted annotations**. The authors of all three genomes used the specialized *Companion* annotation pipeline (developed by the Sanger Institute and integrated tightly with PlasmoDB) before submitting their files to NCBI. 

*(*Note: The older Salvador-I genome is the only one that has an active RefSeq `GCF_` assembly annotated by NCBI's automated pipeline. However, generalized automated pipelines notoriously struggle with the AT-rich, hyper-repetitive subtelomeres of *Plasmodium*, often erroneously merging adjacent *vir* genes or misclassifying them as pseudogenes.)*

So, the counts in the table already represent the official annotations present in both the NCBI GenBank records and PlasmoDB! Would you like me to add a small footnote to the table in `notebook.md` clarifying that these numbers reflect the author-submitted *Companion* annotations mirrored across both databases?
yes, please

The counts above represent fully annotated, functional genes (excluding pseudogenes, which add an additional ~100-116 copies per assembly). Notably, in PvPAM, over 600 of its VIR genes share no direct orthology with PvP01, highlighting the massive geographic diversity of these subtelomeric expansions.*

### Gene and Protein Structures

### PIR (Plasmodium Interspersed Repeat) / VIR
* **Sub-classification:** The *pir* family is highly diverse and is historically subdivided into **distinct subfamilies**. In *P. vivax*, *vir* genes were initially grouped into subfamilies **A through L** (and later expanded/reclassified) based on sequence homology. Similarly, in rodent malarias, *pir* genes are grouped into "S" (short) and "L" (long) groups, each containing distinct numerical subfamilies (e.g., S1-S8, L1-L4). Recent transcriptomic studies show that specific subfamilies are expressed at different stages of infection, suggesting distinct functional roles.
* **Copy Number:** *pir* is the largest multigene family in *Plasmodium*. In *P. vivax*, it has undergone a massive tandem expansion. While the older, short-read Salvador I reference genome identified ~346 *vir* genes, modern long-read assemblies (like the P01 reference) that accurately resolve the highly repetitive subtelomeres have revealed **over 1,000 *vir* copies** per haploid genome.

### PHIST (Plasmodium Helical Interspersed Subtelomeric)
* **Sub-classification:** Based on amino acid composition, sequence homology, and overall gene architecture, the PHIST family is formally divided into three distinct subgroups: **PHISTa**, **PHISTb**, and **PHISTc** (with some additional "PHIST-like" outliers). These subgroups differ in the length of the protein flanking the core PHIST domain and the specific host cytoskeleton targets they bind to.
* **Copy Number:** This family exhibits significant lineage-specific expansion in human and primate malarias compared to rodent models. There are roughly **39 *phist* genes in *P. vivax*** and **~65-72 copies in *P. falciparum***. By stark contrast, rodent malaria models (like *P. berghei* or *P. yoelii*) possess severely contracted families, containing only 1 to 3 copies.

The core consists of beta-strands and alpha-helices organized into a unique scaffold that can tolerate massive amino acid substitutions. This allows the parasite to continuously change its surface "appearance" to immune cells while keeping the protein structurally sound.

By constantly switching which *vir* variants are expressed, the parasite evades the host’s humoral (antibody) immune response. They also play major roles in cytoadherence (making infected red blood cells sticky so they attach to the host's endothelium and avoid clearance in the spleen) and rosetting (binding uninfected red blood cells). In *P. vivax*, *vir* genes are heavily implicated in severe malaria pathogenesis by enabling the parasite to establish chronic, stealthy infections.

These subgroups differ in the length of the protein flanking the core PHIST domain and the specific host cytoskeleton targets they bind to.

Yes, both gene families are formally classified into distinct subgroups based on their sequence homology, domain architecture, and functional traits. I have added this sub-classification breakdown to the `notebook.md`.

Here is how they are grouped:

**PIR / VIR Sub-classification:**
* In *P. vivax*, the *vir* genes were originally grouped into **12 distinct subfamilies (A through L)** based on sequence homology. Subsequent assemblies have expanded and refined these clusters. 
* Across the *Plasmodium* genus (such as in rodent malarias), they are broadly divided by sequence length into **"S" (short)** and **"L" (long)** groups, which are further divided into numbered clusters (e.g., S1-S8, L1-L4). Transcriptomic studies have shown that different subfamilies are expressed at different times during an infection (e.g., acute vs. chronic), implying specialized functional roles for each subgroup.

**PHIST Sub-classification:**
* The PHIST family is formally classified into three main structural subgroups: **PHISTa**, **PHISTb**, and **PHISTc** (along with a few "PHIST-like" outliers). 
* While all subgroups share the core 150-amino acid 4-alpha-helix "PHIST domain", they are separated based on the varying lengths and sequences of the flanking protein regions outside the core domain. These structural differences determine which specific human red blood cell cytoskeleton proteins (like Band 4.1R) or other *Plasmodium* virulence factors (like PfEMP1) the PHIST protein binds to.

1. **PHIST Subgroups (PHISTa, PHISTb, PHISTc):**
   * These subgroups *are* explicitly captured in the genome annotations on both PlasmoDB and NCBI. 
   * For example, in *P. falciparum* (and its orthologs in *P. vivax*), genes are specifically annotated with titles like: `"Plasmodium exported protein (PHISTa), unknown function"` or `"Plasmodium exported protein (PHISTc), unknown function"`. 
   * This is because the PHISTa, b, and c domains are structurally distinct enough that automated Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) run during annotation (like InterProScan/Pfam) can reliably tell them apart and assign the specific subgroup to the gene description.

2. **PIR / VIR Subfamilies:**
   * The annotations for the *pir/vir* family are much looser. In the official PvP01 and PvPAM genome annotations, the vast majority of these genes are simply labeled as `"Plasmodium interspersed repeat protein"` or `"VIR protein, putative"`.
   * **Why?** The *vir* subfamilies (A through L, etc.) are highly dynamic, frequently recombine, and are based on varying sequence homology thresholds rather than strict, universally conserved domains like PHIST. 
   * When authors (like those who assembled the PvPAM and PvP01 genomes) perform their genomic studies, they use specialized clustering algorithms (like OrthoMCL or BLAST networking) *after* the initial annotation to assign them to subfamilies for their published papers. Here is a critique of the proposed approach and why we must be very careful when classifying *vir/pir* genes.

### Critique of the Proposed Approach

The proposed plan relies on using the older **Salvador-I reference genome** as the source for the 12 classical *vir* subfamilies (A through L) and using **sequence homology (BLASTp)** to map the expanded *vir* repertoires of the three modern long-read genomes (PvP01, PvW1, PvPAM) back to those 12 subfamilies.

While conceptually straightforward, this methodology has **three major flaws** in the context of *P. vivax* subtelomeric multigene families:

#### 1. The "12 Subfamilies (A-L)" Classification is Outdated and Incomplete
The classification of *vir* genes into subfamilies A through L was based on the **Salvador-I** genome (published in 2008). 
* Salvador-I was sequenced using older Sanger technology, leaving the highly repetitive subtelomeres massively fragmented. It only captured **~346 *vir* genes**.
* The modern genomes (PvP01, PvW1, PvPAM) contain **over 1,000 *vir* genes**. 
* **The Pitfall:** If we use Salvador-I's A-L subfamilies as our definitive "reference set," we will inevitably fail to classify the hundreds of *vir* genes that were simply missing from Salvador-I. Furthermore, subsequent computational re-evaluations (e.g., Lopez-Perez et al., 2013) have shown that some of the original Salvador-I subfamilies (like A, D, and H) were likely artifacts of the fragmented assembly and shouldn't even be considered true *vir* subfamilies anymore.

#### 2. Extreme Geographic Diversity Defies a Single Reference
Subtelomeric regions undergo constant, rapid recombination (ectopic recombination), creating entirely new chimeric *vir* genes. 
* The PvPAM genome (South America) revealed that **over 600 of its *vir* genes share NO direct orthology** with the PvP01 genome (Indonesia). 
* **The Pitfall:** Because *vir* repertoires are intensely lineage/geography-specific, attempting to force the Indonesian (PvP01), Thai (PvW1), and Peruvian (PvPAM) *vir* genes into the narrow buckets defined by a monkey-adapted Central American strain (Salvador-I) will result in massive numbers of "unclustered" or misclassified genes.

#### 3. Limitations of BLASTp for Multigene Families
Using simple BLASTp to assign subfamilies based on the "best hit" is problematic for tandemly arrayed multigene families.
* *vir* proteins share conserved domains (like the transmembrane domain) but have hyper-variable ectodomains. 
* **The Pitfall:** A BLASTp search will often trigger a "best hit" based on the highly conserved structural backbone rather than the subfamily-defining motifs, leading to false-positive clustering.

---

### Suggested Alternative Methodology

Instead of forcing modern genomes backward into an outdated framework, we should use a **Network-Based or Markov Clustering (MCL)** approach to build the subfamilies *de novo* across the three genomes simultaneously.

**Revised Plan:**
1. **Download Proteomes & Filter:** Fetch the predicted protein sequences for PvP01, PvW1, and PvPAM and extract all annotated PIR/VIR proteins (exactly as proposed).
2. **All-vs-All Homology Search:** Perform an all-versus-all sequence comparison (using MMseqs2 or BLASTp) combining all ~3,300 *vir* proteins from the three genomes into a single pool.
3. **Markov Clustering (MCL):** Use a network clustering algorithm like **MCL** or **OrthoMCL** on the sequence similarity matrix. 
    * By setting a strict inflation parameter, the algorithm will naturally group the proteins into distinct subfamilies based on shared sequence networks.
4. **Subfamily Distribution & Mapping:** 
    * We can then map these newly generated, robust clusters back to the historical Salvador-I "A-L" nomenclature where possible (for backward compatibility with literature).
    * We will quantify how many clusters are shared universally across all three genomes versus how many are continent-specific (e.g., unique to the South American PvPAM).

This network-based approach is the modern gold standard for analyzing *Plasmodium* multigene families and avoids the trap of using an incomplete 15-year-old reference genome to constrain modern long-read data.

cd data/genomes

# Step 2: Extract PIR/VIR proteins from all three genomes and combine them
# PlasmoDB annotations typically use descriptions like "Plasmodium interspersed repeat" or "VIR protein"

conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit grep -r -i -p "plasmodium interspersed repeat|VIR protein" PvP01_proteins.fasta > PvP01_vir.fasta
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit grep -r -i -p "plasmodium interspersed repeat|VIR protein" PvW1_proteins.fasta > PvW1_vir.fasta
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit grep -r -i -p "plasmodium interspersed repeat|VIR protein" PvPAM_proteins.fasta > PvPAM_vir.fasta

# Count the extracted sequences
echo "Extracted VIR sequences:"
echo "PvP01: $(grep -c "^>" PvP01_vir.fasta)"
echo "PvW1: $(grep -c "^>" PvW1_vir.fasta)"
echo "PvPAM: $(grep -c "^>" PvPAM_vir.fasta)"

# Add genome prefixes to headers so we can track origin after clustering
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit replace -p "^>" -r ">PvP01_" PvP01_vir.fasta > PvP01_vir_tagged.fasta
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit replace -p "^>" -r ">PvW1_" PvW1_vir.fasta > PvW1_vir_tagged.fasta
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit replace -p "^>" -r ">PvPAM_" PvPAM_vir.fasta > PvPAM_vir_tagged.fasta

# Combine all into one file
cat PvP01_vir_tagged.fasta PvW1_vir_tagged.fasta PvPAM_vir_tagged.fasta > combined_vir.fasta
echo "Combined total: $(grep -c "^>" combined_vir.fasta)"

arguments.command:
cd data/genomes

# Re-extract using just "PIR protein" and "VIR protein" matching
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit grep -n -r -i -p "PIR protein" -p "VIR protein" PvP01_proteins.fasta > PvP01_vir.fasta
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit grep -n -r -i -p "PIR protein" -p "VIR protein" PvW1_proteins.fasta > PvW1_vir.fasta
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit grep -n -r -i -p "PIR protein" -p "VIR protein" PvPAM_proteins.fasta > PvPAM_vir.fasta

# Count the extracted sequences
echo "Extracted VIR sequences:"
echo "PvP01: $(grep -c "^>" PvP01_vir.fasta)"
echo "PvW1: $(grep -c "^>" PvW1_vir.fasta)"
echo "PvPAM: $(grep -c "^>" PvPAM_vir.fasta)"

# Add genome prefixes to headers
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit replace -p "^>" -r ">PvP01_" PvP01_vir.fasta > PvP01_vir_tagged.fasta
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit replace -p "^>" -r ">PvW1_" PvW1_vir.fasta > PvW1_vir_tagged.fasta
conda run -p ../../.loom/env seqkit replace -p "^>" -r ">PvPAM_" PvPAM_vir.fasta > PvPAM_vir_tagged.fasta

# Combine all into one file
cat PvP01_vir_tagged.fasta PvW1_vir_tagged.fasta PvPAM_vir_tagged.fasta > combined_vir.fasta
echo "Combined total: $(grep -c "^>" combined_vir.fasta)"

content.text:
I've drafted a robust plan (Plan A) in `notebook.md` to classify these VIR genes using an all-vs-all sequence comparison and Markov Clustering (MCL) approach across all three strains combined. This effectively avoids the limitations of the fragmented Salvador-I genome by building the subfamilies *de novo*.

### The Problem with PvW1
While preparing the execution environment locally, I identified a significant snag with the **PvW1** annotation file from PlasmoDB:

*   **PvP01** explicitly labels 1,098 genes as "PIR protein" or "VIR protein".
*   **PvPAM** explicitly labels 1,029 genes as "PIR protein" or "VIR protein".
*   **PvW1** only explicitly labels **49** genes as "VIR protein" in the FASTA headers! 

However, the literature states PvW1 has over 1,145 *vir* genes. 
A quick text search revealed that in the PvW1 annotation file, hundreds of proteins are simply labeled as `unspecified product` or lack the standard `PIR/VIR` gene product strings found in PvP01/PvPAM. 

### How should we proceed?
To fix this before clustering, I can either:
1. **Pfam Domain Filtering (Recommended):** Use a hidden Markov model search (like `hmmsearch` with the Pfam domain for *vir* genes, PF09687) against all "unspecified" proteins in PvW1 to actively recover the missing ~1,100 *vir* sequences.
2. **Drop PvW1:** Proceed with the clustering analysis using only the high-quality PvP01 (Indonesia) and PvPAM (South America) datasets, which represent a solid geographic contrast.

Which path would you like to take?

arguments.command:
cd data/genomes

# Convert TSV format into ABC format required by MCL
# (Column 1: protein 1, Column 2: protein 2, Column 3: bitscore)
awk '{print $1, $2, $3}' combined_vir_aln.tsv > mcl_input.abc

# Run MCL using an inflation parameter of 2.0 (standard for multi-gene families to get moderate granularity)
conda run -p ../../.loom/env mcl mcl_input.abc --abc -I 2.0 -o vir_clusters.txt

# How many clusters did it find?
echo "Number of VIR subfamilies (clusters) identified: $(wc -l < vir_clusters.txt)"
# Show the sizes of the top 15 clusters
echo "Top 15 cluster sizes:"
awk '{print NF}' vir_clusters.txt | sort -nr | head -15

cat << 'EOF' > data/genomes/parse_clusters.py
import pandas as pd
from collections import Counter

clusters = []
with open("vir_clusters.txt") as f:
    for i, line in enumerate(f):
        proteins = line.strip().split()
        if len(proteins) < 3: # Ignore singletons/tiny fragments
            continue
            
        counts = {'Cluster': f"Subfamily_{i+1}", 'PvP01': 0, 'PvW1': 0, 'PvPAM': 0, 'Total': len(proteins)}
        
        for prot in proteins:
            if prot.startswith("PvP01_"):
                counts['PvP01'] += 1
            elif prot.startswith("PvW1_"):
                counts['PvW1'] += 1
            elif prot.startswith("PvPAM_"):
                counts['PvPAM'] += 1
                
        clusters.append(counts)

df = pd.DataFrame(clusters)
df = df.sort_values('Total', ascending=False)

# Print summary for top 20 subfamilies
print(df.head(20).to_string(index=False))

print("\n--- Summary ---")
print(f"Total valid subfamilies (N >= 3): {len(df)}")
print("Distribution of universally shared vs continent-specific subfamilies:")

# Shared across all 3
shared_all = df[(df['PvP01'] > 0) & (df['PvW1'] > 0) & (df['PvPAM'] > 0)]
print(f"Subfamilies present in all 3 genomes: {len(shared_all)}")

# Present in only 1
unique_p01 = df[(df['PvP01'] > 0) & (df['PvW1'] == 0) & (df['PvPAM'] == 0)]
unique_w1 = df[(df['PvW1'] > 0) & (df['PvP01'] == 0) & (df['PvPAM'] == 0)]
unique_pam = df[(df['PvPAM'] > 0) & (df['PvP01'] == 0) & (df['PvW1'] == 0)]

print(f"Subfamilies strictly unique to PvP01 (Indonesia): {len(unique_p01)}")
print(f"Subfamilies strictly unique to PvW1 (Thailand): {len(unique_w1)}")
print(f"Subfamilies strictly unique to PvPAM (Peru): {len(unique_pam)}")

EOF
conda run -p ../../.loom/env python data/genomes/parse_clusters.py
